scenarios.title: Entrepreneurship as a discipline
scenarios.situation: A friend says entrepreneurs are born, not made — 'you either have the risk gene or you don't.' You're studying a curriculum that treats entrepreneurship the way business schools treat finance or marketing: a teachable body of method. Your friend challenges you: if it's teachable, why do most startups still fail?
choices: Entrepreneurship is a method — a repeatable process for discovering problems, testing solutions, and managing uncertainty — and a teachable method still fails often because it operates under irreducible uncertainty: the method improves your odds and your cost per experiment, it doesn't remove risk.
Your friend is right; the curriculum is just motivational speaking with tuition attached.
Most startups fail because founders didn't take enough risk; the method says to bet bigger.
The method guarantees success if followed exactly; failures come from skipping steps.
scenarios.why: Treating entrepreneurship as a discipline means there are learnable skills — customer discovery, unit economics, MVP design — that separate deliberate founders from gamblers. But the domain is uncertainty itself: even perfect method leaves market risk, timing risk, and competition. The discipline's promise is cheaper, faster, more informative failures — more at-bats per dollar — not certainty.
scenarios.hint: Does a good batting coach guarantee every hit?

scenarios.title: The foundations audit
scenarios.situation: You've built a prototype people like, but every business conversation exposes a gap: you can't read the P&L a potential partner sends, your 'marketing plan' is 'post on social media,' and you have no idea what fulfilling 1,000 orders would actually cost. A mentor says to pause and audit your foundations.
scenarios.prompt: What does the foundations audit cover, and why does it come before scaling the prototype?
choices: Finance (can you read statements and model cash), marketing (do you know your customer, channel, and message), and operations (can you deliver at volume, at cost) — because a beloved prototype with broken foundations scales losses, not a business.
It covers pitch-deck design, logo refinement, and social media growth hacks.
It covers finding a technical co-founder; everything else can be outsourced later.
Foundations don't matter until Series A; early stage is only about the product.
scenarios.why: The three foundations map to the three ways startups die after product-market fit: they run out of cash (finance), they can't acquire customers repeatably (marketing), or they can't deliver what they sold (operations). Auditing them before scaling is triage: each gap has a learn-or-hire answer, but an unaudited gap becomes the company's cause of death.
scenarios.hint: Which of the three foundations kills the company if the prototype succeeds?

scenarios.title: Problem discovery before product
scenarios.situation: A founder has spent four months building an app for restaurant scheduling. They've spoken to zero restaurant managers. When you suggest customer interviews, they say 'I already know the problem — I worked in a restaurant in college' and 'talking to people will just slow me down.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the specific failure mode here, and what should happen instead?
choices: Solution-first building on an unvalidated problem: four months of engineering on an assumed pain. The fix is problem discovery — structured interviews with the actual buyers to learn whether the pain is real, urgent, and budgeted — before writing more code.
The failure is not building fast enough; they should add features to differentiate.
The failure is not having a co-founder; solo founders can't do discovery.
Interviews are fine but the real validation is a bigger launch with more users.
scenarios.why: Working in a restaurant gave them a hypothesis, not evidence. Problem discovery interviews test whether the pain is frequent, expensive, and owned by someone with budget — the three properties that make a problem worth solving. Code is the most expensive way to test a hypothesis; conversations are the cheapest. The MVP discipline starts by refusing to build until the problem earns it.
scenarios.hint: What three properties make a customer problem worth building for?

scenarios.title: The unit economics trap
scenarios.situation: A subscription startup celebrates: 10,000 users, growing 20% monthly, 'profitable on paper' because this month's revenue finally exceeded this month's ad spend. You look closer: customer acquisition cost is $60, average customer lifetime is 4 months at $10/month margin, and churn is accelerating.
scenarios.prompt: What is the real unit economics verdict?
choices: The business loses money on every customer: lifetime value is 4 × $10 = $40 against a $60 acquisition cost — LTV/CAC is 0.67, below the 1.0 breakeven and far below the 3.0 healthy threshold. Growth is scaling losses; the celebration is premature.
It's profitable: revenue exceeded ad spend this month, which is the definition of profitability.
The 20% growth rate compensates; unit economics don't matter at this stage.
Churn doesn't matter as long as new users keep arriving faster.
scenarios.why: Unit economics ask one question: does one customer, over their whole lifetime, pay back what they cost to acquire? LTV = $40, CAC = $60, so each new customer destroys $20 of value and 20% growth just destroys it faster. 'Revenue beat ad spend this month' confuses a single month's cash timing with the lifetime math. Fix churn or CAC before spending another dollar on growth.
scenarios.hint: Compute LTV from the numbers given. Is it above or below CAC?

scenarios.title: Reading the term sheet
scenarios.situation: After a long fundraise, you receive your first term sheet: a $2M raise on an $8M pre-money valuation, with a 1x liquidation preference, pro-rata rights for the investor, and a board seat. Your co-founder says 'valuation is all that matters — $8M pre is great, sign it.'
scenarios.prompt: What should you actually evaluate before signing?
choices: The full economics and control package: your post-money ownership ($2M on $8M pre = 20% dilution before option pool), what the 1x liquidation preference means in a modest exit, the option pool shuffle (whose shares fund the employee pool), board control, and protective provisions — valuation is one term among many that determine what you actually keep and control.
Valuation only; the other terms are standard boilerplate that never matters.
Only the board seat matters; economics sort themselves out.
Reject it; any dilution above 10% is unacceptable at this stage.
scenarios.why: A $2M raise on $8M pre-money means you sell 20% of the company — and the option pool, typically topped up pre-money, comes out of the founders' share, not the investors'. The 1x liquidation preference decides who gets paid first in a $5M exit (not you, fully). Fundraising literacy means reading every term as dilution, downside protection, or control — then negotiating the package, not the headline number.
scenarios.hint: If the company sells for $5M, who gets paid first under a 1x preference?

scenarios.title: Borrowing from practitioner models
scenarios.situation: You're accepted to a practitioner-led founder program modeled on the contemporary academy approach: operators teach, the curriculum centers on AI-era building, and hiring partners recruit from graduates. The cost is 6% equity. A friend says 'never give up equity for education' — but your alternative is learning alone for a year.
scenarios.prompt: How do you evaluate the offer?
choices: Price the 6% against the specific, verifiable value: the instructors' operating track records, the hiring partners' actual placement rates, the curriculum's relevance to what you're building, and your opportunity cost of a solo year — take it only if the expected acceleration exceeds 6% of the company's eventual value, and verify every claim before signing.
Always take it; networks are everything and equity is free at this stage.
Never take it; equity is the most expensive currency and education should be free.
Decide based on the program's marketing and demo-day hype videos.
scenarios.why: Practitioner-led education can compress years of mistakes into months — but 6% of a successful company is an enormous tuition. The evaluation is arithmetic plus diligence: expected value of acceleration (faster to revenue, better hires, fewer fatal mistakes) versus 6% of terminal value, with every placement and instructor claim verified against graduate outcomes, not brochures. 'What to borrow, what to avoid' is a due-diligence question, not an ideology.
scenarios.hint: What would the 6% be worth if the company exits at $50M?

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Entrepreneurship as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track failure in Entrepreneurship.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track
evidence: All Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: Find the Bottleneck
scenarios.situation: Your SaaS startup's numbers: 10,000 site visitors/month, 800 trial signups, 40 paying customers, and a support team drowning in tickets from those 40. The marketing lead wants double the ad budget; the product lead wants onboarding fixes; support wants two more hires.
scenarios.prompt: Where is the binding constraint, and what gets the next dollar?
choices: Activation — 800 trials converting to 40 paid (5%) is the leak; fix onboarding before spending another ad dollar
Operations — the support team is drowning; hire first so growth does not collapse service
Revenue — raise prices on the 40 customers to fund everything else
Acquisition — 10,000 visitors is too few; double the ad budget to feed the top of the funnel
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The trial-to-paid conversion of 5% is the constraint: doubling visitors doubles trials but still converts at 5%, doubling churn along the way. Fix activation first, then the same ad budget yields twice the customers. Support pain is real but it is a symptom of serving poorly-activated customers — and hiring into a broken flow just scales the breakage.
scenarios.hint: Which stage, if fixed, multiplies the value of every other stage's effort?
objectives: Trace multi-stage flows to find constraints
evidence: tickets concentrated in first 30 days post-purchase

scenarios.title: The Referral Flywheel
scenarios.situation: Your operations team just cut onboarding time from 14 days to 3 and doubled first-month satisfaction scores. The marketing lead says 'great, now back to ads' — but you see something in the system diagram.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage move this improvement unlocked?
choices: Bank the savings — cut support headcount since tickets will fall
Redirect the operations budget into paid acquisition to scale faster
Build a referral engine on the satisfaction spike — delighted new customers are your cheapest acquisition channel
Raise prices immediately to capture the added value
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Operations improvements feed back into acquisition through reputation and referrals — that is the loop closing. A referral engine converts the satisfaction spike into compounding, near-free acquisition. Cutting headcount (A) or raising prices (D) extracts value once; the flywheel compounds it. This is systems thinking: the improvement's highest value is not where it happened, it is one loop around.
scenarios.hint: Where does the output of this improvement go next in the four-stage flow?
objectives: Convert operational wins into acquisition assets
Think in compounding, not one-time gains
evidence: currently 4% of new customers refer someone

scenarios.title: Fix the Leak or Fill the Funnel?
scenarios.situation: Monthly churn is 9% — you lose nearly 1 in 11 customers every month. Growth has stalled at 500 customers despite healthy new signups. The board is split: half want a retention task force, half want a bigger sales team.
scenarios.prompt: What does the systems view prescribe?
choices: Cut prices to reduce churn — cheaper plans churn less
Both at once — split the budget evenly between retention and acquisition
Hire the sales team — growth covers churn if you sell fast enough
Retention task force first — at 9% monthly churn the bucket cannot be filled; find why customers leave before adding more
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. At 9% monthly churn, average customer lifetime is ~11 months — you are on a treadmill where every new cohort mostly replaces a departing one. Adding sales (C) pours water into a leaking bucket at full CAC cost. The systems move is to diagnose the leak first: exit interviews, usage data, cohort analysis. Only once retention stabilizes does acquisition spend compound instead of evaporate.
scenarios.hint: What is the lifetime value math telling you about where each new customer dollar actually goes?
evidence: flat at 500 customers despite strong signups

scenarios.title: Where Is the Leverage?
scenarios.situation: You have one spare engineering sprint and three candidate projects — a feature 30% of users requested, cutting checkout steps from 5 to 2, and a 5% price increase test on new signups. Current checkout conversion is 22%.
scenarios.prompt: Which project has the highest expected leverage on revenue?
choices: Checkout simplification — conversion is the revenue gate and 22% leaves enormous headroom
The price test — 5% more revenue per customer with zero product work
Split the sprint across all three to keep everyone happy
The requested feature — 30% of users asked for it, so it must matter most
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. A 5% price increase flows almost entirely to margin with no engineering complexity and no funnel dependency — it is pure leverage if demand holds. Checkout work (A) is real but uncertain in magnitude; the feature (D) is requested but requests do not equal willingness to pay. Leverage = effect size divided by effort and risk, and the price test wins that ratio decisively. Test it on a cohort first to verify demand elasticity.
scenarios.hint: Which option changes revenue with the least effort and the least dependence on other stages?
objectives: Separate requests from willingness to pay
evidence: 30% of users requested; no pricing signal attached

scenarios.title: Build Your Study Plan
scenarios.situation: You have three weeks before your exam/interview. There are 15 domains, each with lessons, labs, and scenarios, plus a capstone and a mock assessment.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-leverage way to sequence your preparation?
choices: Follow the domain order, doing lessons then labs then scenarios per domain, with weekly mock assessments to calibrate — compounding foundations with regular full-scope rehearsal
Do all scenarios first to 'see what the test is like,' then go back and read lessons for the ones you missed
Skip to the capstone immediately since it's the most impressive, then fill in theory later
Study only the domains you already know to maximize your confidence going in
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Sequenced foundations compound: each domain's scenarios assume prior domains' vocabulary. Weekly mocks give you a calibrated readiness signal instead of a last-minute surprise. The other options either invert the learning order, skip foundations, or optimize for comfort over growth.
scenarios.hint: Think about what each activity assumes. What breaks if you do scenarios before lessons?
evidence: Weakest areas: unknown — no baseline yet

scenarios.title: Hear the Real Pain
scenarios.situation: Your interviews keep producing compliments ('great idea!') but zero pre-orders. You're confused.
choices: Bad questions: compliments and hypotheticals ('would you use it?') produce flattery, not data — switch to past-behavior questions ('what did you last pay?') and watch for the Mom Test failures in your script
The idea is bad — kill it
Interview more friends — you need encouragement
Lower the price — it's too expensive
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Compliments-without-orders is the classic bad-question signature: your script invited flattery instead of behavior. The Mom Test diagnoses it — rewrite every question to be unflatterable, then re-interview strangers about past spending.
scenarios.hint: What did your questions reward — honesty or politeness?
evidence: 'Would you use this? Do you like it?'

scenarios.title: Climb the Ladder
scenarios.situation: You want to build a $50k platform. You have $5k and no validation.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct first rung?
choices: Problem interviews (free), then a landing page with pre-orders ($100) — earn each rung's evidence before spending the next rung's money; the $50k build is rung 5, not rung 1
Build the $50k platform — go big
Raise money first, validate later
Build a slightly cheaper $30k version
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The MVP ladder exists because each rung costs 5-10× the last — skipping rungs burns capital on unvalidated assumptions. $5k funds rungs 1-3 easily; the evidence from those rungs either justifies raising for rung 5 or saves you $45k.
scenarios.hint: What evidence would justify spending $50k — and what's the cheapest way to get it?

scenarios.title: Name the Pivot
scenarios.situation: Metrics are flat after four real experiments. The team debates: try harder, or change direction?
choices: Pivot, and name the type: four flat experiments exhaust the current strategy's learning — identify which assumption failed and pivot its type (segment, channel, model); 'try harder' without a new hypothesis is sunk-cost drift
Try harder — effort solves everything
Shut down immediately — flat means dead
Change everything at once — fresh start
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Pivot-or-persevere is decided by leading metrics after genuine experiments: flat after four = the strategy is wrong, not the effort. Naming the pivot type focuses the change on the failed assumption instead of random flailing.
scenarios.hint: What did the four experiments actually test — and what did they prove?

scenarios.title: Segment by Behavior
scenarios.situation: Your 'target market' is 'millennials interested in fitness' — 70 million people. Marketing is unfocused.
choices: Behavioral wedge: 'people who paid for a fitness app in the last 90 days and churned' — a reachable, motivated segment with demonstrated budget; expand from the wedge after winning it
Keep it broad — bigger market is better
Narrow to 'my friends who work out'
Segment by zodiac sign for fun
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Demographic mega-segments aren't targets — they're census categories. Behavioral segments (recent payers, churners, active seekers) identify people with demonstrated intent and budget. Win the wedge, then expand: that's how segments become markets.
scenarios.hint: Who has already demonstrated they'll pay for adjacent solutions?

scenarios.title: Prove Willingness to Pay
scenarios.situation: Survey: 80% 'would definitely use' your free beta. You need to know if they'll pay $30/month.
choices: Pre-order test: landing page with pricing and a pay-now (or deposit) button — money movement is the only willingness-to-pay evidence; 80% 'would use' predicts nothing about $30/month
More surveys with pricing questions
Ask them directly if $30 is fair
Assume 80% converts
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Stated willingness-to-pay is worthless — the intention-behavior gap eats surveys alive. Only money movement (pre-orders, deposits, paid pilots) measures actual WTP. Price the test at the real price; discounted tests measure the wrong thing.
scenarios.hint: What has the respondent risked in each test — words or money?

scenarios.title: The Feature Request Trap
scenarios.situation: Your beta users keep requesting the same feature: a reporting dashboard. The loudest three customers say they will churn without it. Your roadmap says the onboarding revamp matters more. Engineering can do one.
choices: Build the dashboard — three customers threatening churn is a fire, put it out
Ignore them — the roadmap is the roadmap, founders must have conviction

Interview the requesters about the job behind the request: what decision does the dashboard serve? You may find a smaller fix (a weekly email export) solves the churn threat without derailing the roadmap
Build both — work weekends, keep everyone happy
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Feature requests are solution proposals from people unqualified to design your product — the job behind the request is the real data. 'Churn threats' over a dashboard often dissolve when the underlying need (a number for Monday's meeting) gets a cheaper solution. Building on demand (A) lets customers design your roadmap; ignoring (B) confuses conviction with deafness; both (D) burns the team for unvalidated work.
scenarios.hint: What job is the dashboard hired to do — and is there a smaller hire that does it?
objectives: Test churn threats against cheaper fixes
Protect the roadmap from loud minorities

domains.name: Business Models: How Money Flows

scenarios.title: Find the Riskiest Block
scenarios.situation: Your canvas is filled: nine blocks, all plausible. You have one month to de-risk.
choices: Rank blocks by risk × consequence: usually value proposition ('does anyone want this?') and revenue ('will they pay?') — test the riskiest assumption first; validating safe blocks first is procrastination
Test the easiest block first — quick wins
Test all blocks simultaneously
Skip testing — the canvas looks solid
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Canvas blocks aren't equal — value and revenue assumptions kill most ventures, so they get tested first. Testing safe blocks first feels productive while the lethal assumptions wait. Risk-ranked testing is the discipline.
scenarios.hint: Which assumption, if wrong, kills the venture?

scenarios.title: Check the Units
scenarios.situation: Your SaaS: $40/mo price, $25/mo COGS+support, $120 CAC. Growth is strong. You're raising to scale.
choices: Contribution $15/mo → LTV (24-mo avg) $360 → LTV:CAC = 3.0 — borderline healthy; payback 8 months; scale cautiously while improving retention or lowering CAC — growth multiplies these exact economics
Strong growth means healthy — scale aggressively
The units don't matter at this stage
Cut price to grow faster
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The unit math: $15 monthly contribution, 3.0 LTV:CAC (at the threshold), 8-month payback. Scaling multiplies this — good if improving, fatal if degrading. 'Growth covers economics' is how startups scale their way into the ground.
scenarios.hint: What does each new customer contribute — and what does growth multiply?

scenarios.title: Pick the Model
scenarios.situation: Your expertise product could be: $5k consulting engagements, $99/mo subscription content, or a 10% marketplace take-rate.
choices: Match model to strengths and math: consulting monetizes expertise immediately but caps on hours; subscription compounds but needs churn control; marketplace needs liquidity first — pick the one whose economics and requirements fit your current assets, then model all three
Do all three at once — diversify
Pick the trendiest — marketplaces are hot
Pick the easiest — consulting
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Model selection is fit-to-assets: consulting converts expertise to cash now; subscription needs content engines and churn discipline; marketplaces need both sides before take-rate matters. Modeling all three exposes the trade-offs; 'do everything' splits focus fatally.
scenarios.hint: What assets do you actually have — expertise, audience, or liquidity?

scenarios.title: Price on Value
scenarios.situation: Your product saves clients $50k/year. You price at $2k (cost-plus). Sales are slow — prospects say it 'seems cheap for what it claims.'
choices: Underpricing signals low value: at $2k against a $50k outcome, the price contradicts the claim — value-based pricing ($8-12k, capturing a fraction of created value) aligns price with promise and funds proper delivery
Lower to $1k — cheaper sells more
The product is the problem, not the price
Offer it free to build traction
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Price is positioning: $2k for $50k of value reads as 'too good to be true' — prospects discount the claim to match the price. Value-based pricing (10-20% of created value) makes the price evidence for the promise. 'Seems cheap for what it claims' is the diagnosis in the prospect's own words.
scenarios.hint: What does your price tell prospects about your claims?

scenarios.title: Stop the Leak
scenarios.situation: SaaS: 200 new customers/month, 5% monthly churn. Net growth is stalling despite strong acquisition.
scenarios.prompt: What is the math and the fix?
choices: Leaky bucket: 5% monthly churn halves the base every ~13 months — acquisition fills a leaking bucket; fix retention (onboarding, value realization, save plays) before scaling acquisition — net revenue retention is the metric
Acquire more — outrun the churn
Churn is normal — ignore it
Raise prices to offset
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The math is brutal: 5% monthly churn = ~46% annual — you re-acquire nearly half your base yearly just to stand still. Retention fixes (onboarding, time-to-value, expansion) compound; acquisition spending on a leaky bucket burns. NRR > 100% is the goal.
scenarios.hint: How many months until half your customers are gone at 5% monthly?

scenarios.title: The Marketplace Chicken-and-Egg
scenarios.situation: You are launching a two-sided marketplace: homeowners and vetted contractors. No contractors will join without homeowner demand; no homeowners will come without contractor supply. You have $40k to solve the cold start.
choices: Split the $40k evenly: ads for both sides simultaneously
Buy supply first: pay 50 contractors a signup bonus to list, then market to homeowners with real inventory
Constrain the market: launch in one neighborhood, manually recruit 20 contractors and 100 homeowners yourself, prove the transaction loop before spending on scale
Build more features to attract both sides organically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Marketplaces cold-start through concentration, not capital: one dense geography where supply and demand can actually meet, built by hand. Split ads (A) spreads $40k across two sides in a wide area — nobody meets anyone. Paid supply (B) buys listings, not transactions. Features (D) do not solve liquidity. Constrain, hand-build liquidity, prove the loop, then expand the geography.
scenarios.hint: Where can $40k create actual meetings between supply and demand — everywhere thinly, or one place densely?
objectives: Prove the loop before scaling spend
evidence: no supply without demand, no demand without supply
