domains.name: Funding and Finance: Capital Strategy

scenarios.title: Choose the Capital
scenarios.situation: Your B2B SaaS is at $30k MRR, growing 10%/mo, profitable on a small team. A VC offers $3M; customers would fund slower growth.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct funding decision?
choices: Assess market physics: if the market is winner-take-all and speed wins, take the capital to capture it; if it's a profitable niche where control and margins matter, bootstrap — decide by market type, not by the offer's flattery
Always take VC money — it's validation
Never take VC money — control is everything
Take it and figure out the strategy later
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The fit test decides: land-grab dynamics + 10× potential = raise; sustainable niche + margin control = bootstrap. $30k MRR profitable gives you the luxury of choice — most founders don't have it. Decide by market physics, because the capital shapes the company to fit its own needs.
scenarios.hint: What does your market reward — speed or efficiency?

scenarios.title: Earn the Next Round
scenarios.situation: You raised a $1.5M seed 14 months ago. Runway: 8 months. Growth is steady but not explosive.
scenarios.prompt: What must the next 8 months prove?
choices: Series A proof: a repeatable growth engine with working unit economics — the seed bought 18-24 months to prove repeatability; with 8 left, every dollar goes to demonstrating the machine, not exploring
Profitability at all costs — cut to survive
Raise a bridge immediately — don't wait
Pivot to something more exciting
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. The ladder logic: seed capital buys proof of repeatability for Series A. With 8 months left, the company must convert steady growth into a demonstrable engine (repeatable acquisition, solid LTV:CAC). Bridge rounds without progress just delay the reckoning.
scenarios.hint: What did the seed money promise to prove — and is it proven?

scenarios.title: Read the Terms
scenarios.situation: Term sheet: $5M at $20M pre, 2× participating preferred, full-ratchet anti-dilution, investor board majority.
choices: Predatory structure: 2× participating means investors take $10M off the top AND share the remainder; full ratchet punishes any down round brutally; board majority cedes control — the $20M headline masks founder-hostile economics
Great — $20M valuation!
Standard terms — sign it
Negotiate only the valuation higher
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Terms dominate valuation: participating preferred double-dips, 2× multiple front-loads investor returns, full ratchet is the harshest anti-dilution, and board majority surrenders governance. A $20M valuation with these terms can pay founders less than a $12M clean term sheet.
scenarios.hint: What do founders actually receive in a $30M exit under these terms?

scenarios.title: Watch the Cash
scenarios.situation: Your model shows profitability in month 18. Payroll is monthly, customers pay quarterly in arrears. Current cash: 4 months of burn.
scenarios.prompt: What kills you despite the model's profit?
choices: Cash timing: quarterly-arrears collections against monthly payroll creates a working-capital gap — profitable on paper, insolvent in month 5 when payroll hits before receivables arrive; the model needs a cash-flow (not P&L) view with collection timing
Nothing — profitability is what matters
The model is wrong about profit
Cut payroll to match collections
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. P&L profit and cash survival are different things: timing mismatches (payroll monthly, collections quarterly) kill profitable companies. The model must include cash-flow timing — the cash-out date under the downside case is the real constraint, not accounting profit.
scenarios.hint: When does the cash actually arrive versus when must it leave?

scenarios.title: Plan the Downside
scenarios.situation: Board meeting: your base case needs everything to go right. The downside case isn't modeled.
choices: Three scenarios with the downside as the operating plan: base (expected), upside (hiring triggers), downside (6+ months buffer, cut triggers defined) — operate to the downside, hope for the base; the board funds prudence, not optimism
Only the base case — confidence matters
Only the upside — think big
No model — models are fiction
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Scenario discipline: the downside case with buffer and pre-defined cut triggers is the operating plan; base is the forecast; upside sets hiring triggers. Boards punish surprise more than conservatism — the downside plan is credibility.
scenarios.hint: What do you do if the base case doesn't happen — and when do you decide?

scenarios.title: The Bridge Round
scenarios.situation: You raised $1.5M eighteen months ago. Growth is decent but not round-worthy: $30k MRR, 8% monthly growth. Cash runs out in 4 months. Your lead investor offers a $500k bridge on a SAFE with a 20% discount — but wants a board seat and monthly reporting.
choices: Shut down — if you cannot raise, the market has spoken
Reject it — bridges signal weakness, go raise the full round now
Take it and relax — 4 more months of runway solves everything

Take it as a tool, not a rescue: accept the bridge, cut burn 20% the same week, and set a hard 90-day milestone (e.g., $50k MRR) that makes the priced round inevitable — bridges buy milestones, not time
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. A bridge is a bet on a specific milestone, not an extension of the status quo: take the capital, cut burn simultaneously (extending its power), and aim every week at the number that unlocks the real round. Rejecting (B) gambles 4 months of runway on a round the metrics do not support; relaxing (C) repeats the exact spending that created the crisis; shutting down (A) surrenders a winnable 90-day sprint.
scenarios.hint: What specific milestone does $500k buy — and what changes on day one to make it achievable?
objectives: Set the round-unlocking number in advance

domains.summary: Bootstrapping vs raising, the funding ladder, term sheets, financial modeling — capital as strategy.

domains.name: Marketing and Growth: Distribution

scenarios.title: Own the Slot
scenarios.situation: Three competitors claim 'AI-powered analytics.' You're launching similar tech. Prospects can't distinguish anyone.
choices: Reposition the category: own a specific outcome-slot ('the analytics that cuts reporting from days to minutes for finance teams') and frame competitors as 'generic dashboards' — specificity beats superlatives when everyone claims the same adjective
Claim 'more AI-powered' than competitors
Compete on price — undercut them
Add more features to differentiate
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. When everyone claims the same attribute, the attribute becomes noise — specificity ('for finance teams,' 'days to minutes') creates the mental slot. Repositioning competitors as the old/generic way makes you the future. Feature-count and price wars are losing games.
scenarios.hint: What slot is actually empty in the prospect's mind?

scenarios.title: Pick the Channel
scenarios.situation: $2k ACV B2B product, tight ICP (5000 companies), 3-month sales cycle. Marketing suggests TikTok virality.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct channel strategy?
choices: Outbound + ABM: high ACV and a countable ICP mean targeted outbound (email/LinkedIn sequences) and account-based plays — TikTok's broad reach mismatches a 5000-account universe; channel must fit deal size and target count
TikTok — virality is free reach
Billboards — brand awareness
Wait for inbound — build it and they come
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Channel-model fit: $2k ACV supports human-touch outbound; 5000 countable accounts enable ABM precision. TikTok optimizes for millions of impressions — wrong geometry for 5000 targets. The channel must match the deal economics.
scenarios.hint: How many potential customers exist — and what does that imply for channel choice?

scenarios.title: Fix the Leak
scenarios.situation: Funnel: 20k visitors → 1k signups (5%) → 100 activated (10%) → 30 paid (30%). Growth is flat.
choices: Signup→activation (90% loss): the leakiest stage — onboarding overhaul (time-to-value, checklists, triggered guidance) — a 2× activation improvement doubles revenue with zero new traffic
More visitors — top of funnel
Redesign the homepage
Lower prices to convert more
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Funnel math: the 90% signup→activation loss dominates — fixing it 2× doubles customers without new traffic. Top-of-funnel fixes multiply through the same leak. Always fix the leakiest stage first; it's the highest-leverage work in the company.
scenarios.hint: Which stage loses the most — and what does fixing it 2× do?

scenarios.title: Compound Retention
scenarios.situation: Two levers: +10% acquisition or +10% retention improvement. Which compounds harder?
choices: Retention: acquisition gains are linear (more in, same leak); retention gains compound across every future cohort — a 10% churn reduction increases LTV multiplicatively and raises the ceiling on all acquisition spend
Acquisition — new customers are growth
They're equal — 10% is 10%
Neither — focus on pricing
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Retention compounds: lower churn raises LTV, which raises allowable CAC, which makes every acquisition dollar more effective — a flywheel. Acquisition without retention is a treadmill: faster running, same place. Cohort math proves it.
scenarios.hint: What happens to cohort 12's value when churn drops 10%?

scenarios.title: Commit to Content
scenarios.situation: Content marketing after 2 months: 500 visits/month, no pipeline. The CEO wants to kill it for paid ads.
choices: Content compounds on a 6-12 month curve: month 2 is the trough of disillusionment — evaluate leading indicators (ranking trajectory, email captures, content-assisted deals) not lagging pipeline; killing at month 2 guarantees the sunk cost with zero asset
Kill it — 2 months is enough to judge
Double content output immediately
Pivot content to viral topics
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Content is a compounding asset with a J-curve: months 1-3 look dead, months 6-12 inflect. Judging at month 2 by pipeline is category error — measure rankings, captures, and assisted influence. Killing now locks in the loss; the asset was 4 months from paying.
scenarios.hint: What does the content curve look like at month 2 vs month 9?

scenarios.title: The Channel Saturates
scenarios.situation: Paid search drove your growth from $0 to $2M ARR at a $120 CAC. This quarter, CAC crept to $210 as competitors bid up your keywords. The channel still works — it just costs 75% more per customer.
choices: Increase the budget — scale cures rising CAC
Kill paid search immediately — the channel is dead
Treat saturation as a portfolio signal: cap search spend at the CAC ceiling your unit economics allow, and reallocate the growth budget to test two new channels against the same CAC bar
Cut prices to improve conversion and offset the CAC rise
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Channel saturation is normal lifecycle, not failure: every channel has a CAC curve, and the discipline is a ceiling (what the unit economics allow) plus continuous testing of the next channel. More budget (A) buys increasingly expensive customers; killing it (B) discards a working channel; price cuts (D) sacrifice margin to subsidize a bidding war. Portfolio thinking beats channel loyalty.
scenarios.hint: Is paid search broken — or has it simply moved past the CAC your economics allow?
objectives: Cap channels at economic CAC ceilings
Run growth as a channel portfolio
Test the next channel before you need it
evidence: paid search: CAC $120 → $210, was the growth engine

domains.summary: Positioning, acquisition channels, conversion, retention — how customers find, buy, and stay.

domains.name: Sales: The Revenue Engine

scenarios.title: Diagnose Before Prescribing
scenarios.situation: A rep pitches for 20 minutes, then discovers the prospect lacks budget authority.
choices: Discovery and qualification: BANT before pitch — 20 minutes of presenting to a non-buyer is theater; the 70/30 discovery rule and authority check happen first, always
The pitch wasn't good enough
The product is wrong
The prospect lied
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Process failure: pitching before qualifying wastes the scarcest resource (the rep's time) on unwinnable deals. BANT qualification and discovery-first sequencing prevent exactly this — diagnose before prescribing, qualify before pitching.
scenarios.hint: When should you have learned about authority — minute 2 or minute 20?

scenarios.title: Handle the Price Objection
scenarios.situation: Prospect: 'Your competitor is half the price.' The rep immediately offers 30% off.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response instead?
choices: LAER then value: listen fully, acknowledge price matters, explore what 'half price' includes (features? support? outcomes?), then respond with cost-of-inaction and ROI — discounting first trains price-buying and concedes value
Match the competitor's price
Walk away — price buyers aren't worth it
Offer 40% off to win
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 'Half the price' is a value objection wearing a price mask — LAER diagnoses what the comparison actually covers, then ROI reframes to outcomes. Instant discounting confirms the price was inflated and teaches the market to negotiate everything.
scenarios.hint: What is the prospect really saying — and what do you need to know before responding?

scenarios.title: Systematize Persistence
scenarios.situation: Reps average 2 follow-ups then move on. Industry data says 80% of deals need 5+.
choices: Sequenced cadence in the CRM: 4-6 dated touches with distinct angles (thank-you, insight, check-in, break-up), automated where possible, measured per-rep — persistence systematized, not left to willpower
Tell reps to try harder
Hire more reps
Lower prices to close faster
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Follow-up failure is a systems problem: willpower doesn't scale, sequences do. The 4-6 touch cadence with varied angles, CRM-enforced, converts the 80%-need-5+ reality into process. 'Try harder' isn't a system.
scenarios.hint: Is follow-up a motivation problem or a systems problem?

scenarios.title: Demo Their Tuesday
scenarios.situation: Demos showcase 40 features in 30 minutes. Prospects go quiet. Close rate is 8%.
choices: Rebuild around their use case: 'here's your Tuesday morning' — 3-act structure (their pain, your fix, their future), check-ins every 3 minutes, trial close before proposing; features serve the story, not the other way around
Add more features to the demo
Shorten to 10 minutes of features
Demo without slides — pure improv
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Feature tours don't close — outcome stories do. The 3-act demo makes the prospect the protagonist; check-ins keep them engaged; the trial close tests temperature. 8% close rate on feature tours is the predictable result of product-centric demoing.
scenarios.hint: Whose story does the demo tell — yours or theirs?

scenarios.title: Always Next Steps
scenarios.situation: Calls end with 'let me think about it.' Pipeline is full of thinking-about-its. Nothing closes.
choices: Dated next steps on every interaction: no call ends without a calendar commitment ('I'll send the ROI sheet Tuesday; we review Thursday 2pm?') — 'thinking about it' is a polite no; the calendar is the truth serum
Give them more time to think
Send more materials to think with
Assume they're not interested and move on
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. 'Let me think' without a dated next step is deal death wearing politeness. Every interaction must end with a mutual calendar commitment — it tests real interest and maintains momentum. Pipeline full of undated 'think-about-its' is fiction.
scenarios.hint: What distinguishes a real 'thinking' from a polite no?

scenarios.title: The Champion Leaves
scenarios.situation: Your $180k enterprise deal is in legal review. Your champion — the VP who drove the evaluation — just resigned. The economic buyer (CFO) never met you. The new interim VP wants to 're-evaluate all in-flight vendors.'
choices: Multi-thread immediately: brief the CFO on the business case the champion built, arm the end users who ran the pilot with their results data, and ask the departing champion for a warm handoff — deals with one thread die with the thread
Go over the interim VP's head to the CEO
Discount 20% to make the deal too good to re-evaluate
Wait for the new VP to settle in, then re-pitch from scratch
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Single-threaded deals are hostages to org charts: the rescue is building the threads you should have built earlier — economic buyer, end users with proof, and the departing champion's handoff. Discounting (C) bribes a process that has lost its sponsor; waiting (D) lets the re-evaluation conclude without you; escalation (B) alienates the person now deciding. Multi-threading is both the rescue and the lesson.
scenarios.hint: How many people inside that account would fight for this deal if the champion vanished — and what does that number tell you?
objectives: Sell the business case to the economic buyer
Turn users' pilot data into internal advocacy

domains.summary: Discovery, demos, objection handling, closing — sales as a repeatable process.

domains.name: Operations and Legal: The Foundation

scenarios.title: Choose the Entity
scenarios.situation: Two founders, planning to raise venture capital in 18 months, currently pre-revenue.
choices: Delaware C-corp now: venture investors require it, option pools and acquisitions assume it — forming it now avoids a costly conversion later; add founder vesting with 1-year cliff
LLC — simpler and pass-through
Sole proprietorship — deal with it later
Wyoming DAO LLC — it's trendy
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Entity follows funding path: venture-scale ambitions demand Delaware C-corp from birth — conversion later costs $15-50k and months. Founder vesting protects against co-founder departure. The 'simple now' choices create expensive future surgery.
scenarios.hint: What will your investors require — and what does conversion cost later?

scenarios.title: Own Your IP
scenarios.situation: A contractor built your core product. No written agreement. The contractor now claims ownership.
choices: You likely don't own it: without work-for-hire + IP assignment in writing, contractors generally retain IP in their creations — you're negotiating from weakness; lesson: written IP assignment before work starts, always
You own it — you paid for it
Possession is ownership — you have the code
Sue immediately — you'll win easily
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Payment doesn't transfer IP — written assignment does. This is the most expensive missing-paperwork in startups: the product you can't cleanly own, sell, or fundraise on. The fix is preventive (agreements first); the cure is negotiated and costly.
scenarios.hint: What transfers IP — payment or paperwork?

scenarios.title: Vest the Founders
scenarios.situation: Three founders split equity 33/33/33, no vesting. Six months in, one leaves.
choices: The departed founder keeps 33% forever: without vesting, there's no mechanism to reclaim unearned equity — the remaining founders work for a ghost partner; the fix (4-year vest, 1-year cliff) had to be at formation
The equity returns automatically
You can vote them out and reclaim it
It's fine — they earned it
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Unvested founder equity is a time bomb: the 1-year cliff means leavers-before-a-year get nothing, and 4-year vesting aligns ownership with contribution. Without it, the cap table carries dead equity that punishes future fundraising and team morale.
scenarios.hint: What did the departed founder actually earn in six months?

scenarios.title: See the Cash
scenarios.situation: The P&L shows profit. The bank account is empty. Payroll is Friday.
choices: Cash-flow visibility: P&L profit with empty bank = timing (receivables uncollected, payables due) — the missing system is the 13-week cash forecast and monthly close discipline; profit without cash management is insolvency with good accounting
The accountant is wrong
Profit doesn't matter
Borrow to cover payroll and hope
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Cash and profit are different: profit is accounting, cash is survival. The 13-week forecast makes timing visible; monthly closes catch drift. 'Profitable but broke' is the classic small-business killer — the system that prevents it is financial hygiene, not hope.
scenarios.hint: When does the cash arrive versus when must it leave?

scenarios.title: Hire for the Bottleneck
scenarios.situation: Everything stalls on the founder doing sales. The founder wants to hire a 'visionary COO.'
choices: The bottleneck is sales capacity: hire (or contract) sales execution — a closer, an SDR, a sales process — not a COO; prestigious titles don't relieve constraints, targeted capacity does
Hire the COO — vision matters
Hire 5 interns — cheap capacity
Don't hire — work harder
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Hiring follows the bottleneck: founder-as-sales-bottleneck needs sales capacity, not a COO. The 'visionary' hire is prestige over function. Contractor-first validates the role before headcount commitment. Every hire should name the constraint it relieves.
scenarios.hint: What specifically is stuck — and what role unsticks it?
evidence: Founder is the entire sales function

scenarios.title: Contractor or Employee?
scenarios.situation: Your first 'hire' is a designer working 40 hours a week, on your equipment, attending your standups, paid monthly — classified as a contractor with no benefits. It has been 8 months. They are happy with the arrangement.
choices: Keep it — they are happy, you save on benefits and payroll tax, everyone wins
Convert them to an employee now: 40h/week on your equipment under your direction is the textbook misclassification test, and the penalties compound with every month
Ask them to incorporate as an LLC to make the contractor status official
Reduce their hours to 29/week to stay under the threshold
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Misclassification is judged on the working relationship, not the label or anyone's happiness: direction, control, equipment, and full-time exclusivity all point to employment, and penalties plus back taxes compound monthly. An LLC (C) does not change the substance test; hour-gaming (D) is evasion that auditors see through. Convert now, document the change, and get counsel on the lookback exposure.
scenarios.hint: If an auditor looked at the substance of this relationship — not the label — what would they conclude?
objectives: Fix misclassification before auditors find it

domains.summary: Entity formation, contracts, hiring, and operational systems — the unglamorous work that prevents disaster.

domains.name: Pitch Mastery

scenarios.title: Open With the Customer
scenarios.situation: You have 30 seconds before the partners check their phones. Your current opener: 'We're building an AI-powered workflow automation platform for mid-market companies.'
choices: Keep the platform description but add your funding history for credibility
Open with the customer's pain and cost: 'Mid-market ops teams lose 15 hours a week to manual data entry — $60k a year per team. We give those hours back.'
Open with your team's credentials — ex-FAANG founders signal quality fast
Open with market size — '$40B market' frames the opportunity immediately
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Pain-first openers create attention because they name a cost the listener recognizes; technology-first openers (A) invite tuning out, credentials (C) are better placed on the team slide, and market size (D) is abstract until pain is established. Thirty seconds buys you the next three minutes only if the listener feels the problem.
scenarios.hint: What makes a stranger keep listening past the first sentence — your technology, or their pain?
objectives: Quantify the cost of the status quo
evidence: partners decide in ~30 seconds whether to engage

scenarios.title: Order the Deck
scenarios.situation: Your deck currently runs: team → product → market → problem → traction → financials → ask. A mentor says the order is costing you meetings.
choices: Ask first — lead with the amount so investors can decide fast
Team → ask → everything else — credentials and clarity above all
Alphabetical is fine — investors skip around anyway, so order does not matter
Problem → solution → why now → market → product → traction → business model → team → financials → ask
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. The canonical order is a narrative arc: pain, answer, why-now, opportunity, proof, mechanics, people, numbers, request. Leading with team (current) front-loads credentials before the listener cares; leading with ask (A) demands commitment before establishing value. Familiar order reduces cognitive friction — investors pattern-match, so give them the pattern.
scenarios.hint: Which order tells a story where each slide makes the listener want the next one?
objectives: Reduce cognitive friction with familiar order
evidence: team → product → market → problem → traction → financials → ask

scenarios.title: The Hockey-Stick Question
scenarios.situation: A partner points at your projection slide: 'This hockey stick — $200k to $8M in three years. Walk me through the math.' Your model is top-down: 0.5% of a $1.6B market.
choices: Rebuild the answer bottom-up on the spot: customers × price × retention, naming the assumptions and which ones are proven vs projected
Pivot to vision — 'projections are directional; the opportunity is the story'
Offer to send a detailed spreadsheet after the meeting
Defend the top-down math — 0.5% share is conservative for this market
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Investors test thinking, not prophecy: walking through customers × price × retention shows you understand your own drivers and which assumptions carry the model. Defending top-down fantasy (D) fails the sophistication test; vision-pivoting (B) dodges the question; deferring (C) wastes the live moment when conviction is formed. Name proven vs projected assumptions explicitly — honesty about uncertainty is the sophistication signal.
scenarios.hint: Is the investor asking for the right number, or for proof you understand what drives the number?

scenarios.title: The Hostile Question
scenarios.situation: Mid-pitch, a partner interrupts: 'This is a feature, not a company. The incumbents ship this in a quarter.' The room goes quiet.
choices: Concede the point and move on quickly to avoid dwelling on weakness
Attack the incumbent's competence — they are slow and you know it
Answer directly: name your wedge, why incumbents structurally will not prioritize it, and your path from wedge to platform — then invite them to stress-test it
Promise a broader roadmap that proves you are already a platform
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The three-part structure — direct answer, structural reason incumbents will not follow, wedge-to-platform path — turns an attack into your strongest moment. Conceding (A) surrenders the frame; attacking (B) looks defensive; promising a platform roadmap (D) confirms their critique that you are unfocused. Composure plus a crisp wedge argument is exactly what 'can this founder handle pressure' questions are screening for.
scenarios.hint: What is the question actually testing — your roadmap, or your composure and strategic clarity?
objectives: Answer attacks with structure, not defensiveness
Defend the wedge, then show the platform path
Treat hostility as a composure screen

scenarios.title: The Cold Email Pitch
scenarios.situation: You are emailing 50 seed investors you have never met. Your draft is 400 words covering the full story arc, team bios, and financials.
choices: The full 400-word version — investors need complete information to decide
A 120-word note: one-line pain, one-line solution + traction proof, one-line why-you, and a single clear ask for 20 minutes
A deck attachment with no body text — the deck speaks for itself
A long personal story about your founder journey — authenticity wins
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Cold email is a trailer, not the film: 120 words respecting the investor's time, with proof (traction) doing the persuading and one frictionless ask. Full-story emails (A) do not get read; bare attachments (C) feel like spam; founder-journey essays (D) center you instead of the opportunity. The reply is the conversion event — optimize the email for the reply, not for completeness.
scenarios.hint: What is the email optimizing for — informing the investor, or earning a 20-minute call?
objectives: Lead with proof, end with one ask

scenarios.title: Demo Day Timing
scenarios.situation: Demo day gives you 5 minutes on stage plus 2 for questions, in front of 200 investors. Your rehearsal runs 9 minutes and you keep rushing the traction slide.
choices: Talk faster — the content is all essential
Cut the product demo — slides are safer under time pressure
Cut to one story: problem (60s), shift (30s), traction proof (90s), ask (60s) — one customer story carries the product, the demo becomes a 20-second clip
Skip Q&A prep — stage time is what matters
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Five minutes forces one story told well, not a compressed ten-slide deck — and rushing the traction slide (the hinge) destroys the highest-value 90 seconds. A single customer story carries problem, product, and proof together; a 20-second demo clip shows without risking live failure. Talking faster (A) signals panic; cutting the demo (B) removes your most persuasive asset; skipping Q&A prep (D) wastes the highest-intent minutes.
scenarios.hint: If you only had 90 seconds, which slide would you keep — and what does that tell you about the other 7 minutes?
objectives: Design for the time box, not the content
Let one story carry multiple slides' jobs
Protect the traction minutes at all costs

scenarios.title: The Valuation Question
scenarios.situation: An interested angel asks: 'What valuation are you raising at?' You have no lead investor and no priced round yet — you planned a SAFE with a cap but have not set it.
choices: Refuse to discuss valuation until they commit — information advantage
Name a high number to anchor — 'we're raising at $12M' sets expectations
Name a low number to seem like a bargain — 'we'll take $4M' gets checks faster
Defer to the market: 'We're raising $750k on a SAFE; we're letting the round set the cap with our lead — what range would work for you?'
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Without a lead, naming a number either anchors too high (killing interest) or too low (leaving money and signaling weakness); deferring to the round's formation while naming the instrument and amount keeps you credible and invites the investor into price discovery. The question is often a test of founder maturity around fundraising mechanics — handling it collaboratively beats both anchoring games and stonewalling.
scenarios.hint: Who should set the price when there is no lead — and what does naming a number prematurely cost you?
objectives: Let the lead set price discovery
Treat valuation questions as maturity tests
Stay collaborative on mechanics, firm on vision
evidence: $750k planned, SAFE, no cap set, no lead

scenarios.title: The Silent Investor
scenarios.situation: A partner said 'interesting — send me the deck and your numbers' two weeks ago. You sent everything next day. Silence since. Your co-founder says wait; your advisor says ping weekly.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right follow-up play?
choices: Send one crisp update with genuine news (a customer win, a metric moved) and a specific next step; then put them on a monthly update list regardless of reply
Write them off and never contact them again
Wait — pushing a partner who went quiet looks desperate
Email daily until they respond — persistence is the job
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Silence usually means timing or priority, not rejection — a news-driven nudge gives them a reason to re-engage without pleading, and the monthly update list keeps you in orbit until their thesis or calendar changes. Waiting passively (C) surrenders the relationship; daily emails (D) burn it; writing them off (B) discards an already-warmed contact. The follow-up machine runs on genuine progress, which is why shipping between meetings matters.
scenarios.hint: What gives a silent investor a reason to re-engage — another 'checking in', or news?
objectives: Follow up with news, not nudges
Keep warm contacts in orbit with updates
Treat silence as timing, not verdict
evidence: co-founder says wait, advisor says ping weekly

domains.summary: Crafting and delivering pitches that raise capital.

domains.name: Growth Analytics

scenarios.title: The CAC Alarm
scenarios.situation: Your blended CAC is $180 and blended LTV is $700 — a healthy-looking 3.9:1 ratio. But growth has stalled and cash is tightening. You segment by channel and find: organic CAC $40 (LTV $900), paid social CAC $310 (LTV $420).
scenarios.prompt: What does the segmented truth demand?
choices: Reallocate: scale organic aggressively, fix or kill paid social — its 1.35:1 ratio destroys value on every customer
Raise prices to fix the paid social ratio
Celebrate — 3.9:1 blended is healthy, stay the course
Kill paid social immediately and cut all marketing spend
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Paid social acquires customers at $310 against $420 of lifetime value — a 1.35:1 ratio that loses money on every marginal customer, hidden inside a healthy blended average. The blended number is the lie; the segments are the truth. Reallocation (scale what works, fix-or-kill what does not) is the systems move. Killing all marketing (D) starves the $40-CAC engine; price hikes (B) treat a channel problem as a pricing problem.
scenarios.hint: Which number describes a real customer — the blended average, or the channel they came through?

scenarios.title: Fix the Funnel
scenarios.situation: Your funnel: 20,000 visitors → 4,000 signups (20%) → 400 activated (10%) → 160 paying (40%). The team debates: SEO for more visitors, or onboarding work for activation.
choices: More visitors — 20% signup conversion is fine, feed the top
Signup flow — 20,000 to 4,000 loses the most people in absolute terms
Activation — 4,000 signups collapsing to 400 activated is the catastrophic leak; fixing it multiplies every upstream effort
Pricing — 40% trial-to-paid is low, discount to convert more
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Activation loses 3,600 of 4,000 signups — the largest absolute loss and the stage that multiplies all upstream spend. Doubling visitors (A) at 10% activation just doubles the waste; signup-flow work (B) optimizes a stage converting at a healthy 20%. Fix activation first and the same 20,000 visitors yield multiples more revenue — that is leverage.
scenarios.hint: Which stage, if doubled, multiplies the value of all the traffic you already buy?
objectives: Read the whole funnel, not one rate
evidence: SEO for visitors vs onboarding for activation

scenarios.title: Read the Cohort
scenarios.situation: Your March cohort shows 71% month-2 retention vs 58% for February. The product team credits the new onboarding flow shipped March 1. But March also brought a pricing change: annual plans discounted 20%, and annual buyers historically retain better.
choices: Average them — both changes happened, both deserve some credit
Credit onboarding — 13 points is a massive lift, ship the celebration post
Credit pricing — annual buyers retain better, the discount explains everything
Segment before concluding: compare March monthly-plan cohort vs February monthly-plan cohort to isolate onboarding from the pricing mix shift
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Two changes landed simultaneously — onboarding revamp and a pricing mix shift toward stickier annual buyers — so the raw cohort lift is confounded. Comparing like-with-like (monthly-plan cohorts across months) isolates the onboarding effect. Crediting onboarding (B) risks celebrating a mix shift; crediting pricing (C) risks ignoring a real product win; averaging (A) is analytical surrender. Cohorts are only truth-tellers when segments are clean.
scenarios.hint: What changed between February and March besides the onboarding flow?
objectives: Control for confounders in cohort reads
Distinguish mix shifts from real improvement
evidence: Mar: annual discount → stickier buyer mix

scenarios.title: Kill the Test Early?
scenarios.situation: Day 4 of a 14-day pricing test: the new price shows +18% conversion with 400 visitors per variant. Your co-founder wants to ship it now and move on.
choices: Kill the test — pricing tests are too risky to run at all
Hold the line: 400 visitors cannot reliably detect an 18% lift; let it run the full 14 days per the pre-registered rule, then decide
Extend the test to 30 days to be extra safe
Ship it — +18% on 400 visitors is a clear win, speed matters
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Early results fluctuate wildly — day-4 lifts routinely evaporate by day 14 as novelty effects fade and samples stabilize. The pre-registered 14-day rule exists precisely to prevent emotion-driven shipping. Shipping now (D) risks locking in noise; killing tests entirely (A) abandons learning; extending arbitrarily (C) moves the goalposts. Discipline is honoring the card you wrote before the data tempted you.
scenarios.hint: Why did you write a 14-day rule before launch — and what is it protecting you from right now?

scenarios.title: Attribution Dispute
scenarios.situation: Last-click attribution says paid search drives 60% of signups; first-click says your content program drives 55%. The content lead and the search lead each claim the budget.
choices: Trust first-click — awareness is the scarce asset
Split the budget by the average of the two models
Trust last-click — the final touch before signup is what converted them
Run a holdout: pause search in two comparable regions for a month and measure the true signup delta — fund by marginal CAC, not model credit
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Attribution models allocate credit; holdouts measure causality. Pausing search regionally reveals its true marginal contribution — often far below last-click credit, because high-intent buyers would have found you anyway. Averaging models (B) averages two distortions; picking a model (C, A) picks a bias. The budget follows marginal CAC from experiments, not credit from models.
scenarios.hint: Do the models measure what caused the signup, or just what touched the buyer last or first?
objectives: Treat models as lenses, not truth

scenarios.title: The Vanity Metric
scenarios.situation: The board deck headline: '100,000 app downloads, up 300%!' But revenue is flat, DAU is 2,000, and the growth lead wants a bigger budget to 'keep the momentum'.
choices: Approve the budget — 300% growth in downloads is momentum by definition
Replace the headline metric: report activated users, retention, and revenue per download — then size the budget against those
Stop all acquisition until downloads convert better
Rebrand downloads as 'community reach' so the number still shines
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Downloads without activation are inventory, not growth — 2% DAU on 100k downloads means the funnel converts attention into almost nothing. The metric you headline is the behavior you incentivize; headlining downloads buys more downloads. Reframe the dashboard around activation, retention, and revenue, then fund what moves those. Approving on vanity (A) or rebranding (D) institutionalizes the distortion; freezing acquisition (C) treats a measurement problem as a strategy problem.
scenarios.hint: If downloads tripled again and revenue stayed flat, would the company be healthier?
objectives: Headline metrics that tie to revenue

scenarios.title: Payback vs Growth
scenarios.situation: An enterprise channel offers CAC $5,000 with LTV $30,000 (6:1, excellent) but a 22-month payback. You have 14 months of runway and no profitable base to fund the gap.
choices: Test small with strict guardrails: pilot 10 customers, require upfront annual prepay to compress payback, and only scale if payback drops under 12 months
Raise a bridge round to fund the payback gap
Scale it — 6:1 LTV:CAC is elite, the math will work out
Reject the channel entirely — 22-month payback is disqualifying
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Great ratios with lethal payback are a cash-flow trap: you go broke waiting for the LTV to arrive. But rejecting (D) discards a 6:1 channel that annual prepay could salvage — prepay converts the payback problem into a working-capital solution. The pilot tests whether customers will actually prepay before you bet the company. Scaling blind (C) or raising to fund a trap (B) both gamble survival on timing.
scenarios.hint: What kills you first here — the ratio, or the calendar?
objectives: Treat payback as a survival constraint

scenarios.title: The Experiment Backlog
scenarios.situation: The growth team proposes 12 experiments for next quarter: new headlines, pricing tests, referral program, onboarding revamp, email sequences, chatbot, and six more. Engineering can support 3.
choices: Let the team vote — democratic prioritization builds buy-in
Pick the 3 cheapest to run — maximize experiment count per sprint
Score each by expected value (reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort) against the funnel's biggest leak, and run the top 3 — likely the onboarding revamp and pricing tests first
Do the referral program — virality is the highest-leverage growth of all
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Expected-value scoring against the binding constraint turns a wish list into a portfolio: reach × impact × confidence ÷ effort, aimed at the funnel's biggest leak. Voting (A) optimizes for popularity; cheapest-first (B) optimizes for activity over impact; defaulting to virality (D) chases a tactic without evidence it fits this product. Three well-chosen experiments beat twelve scattered ones.
scenarios.hint: Which three experiments attack the constraint — and how do you know, rather than feel?

domains.summary: Metrics, funnels, and experiments that drive growth.

domains.name: Team Leadership

scenarios.title: Generalist or Specialist?
scenarios.situation: You are hiring employee #6. The bottleneck is clear: nobody owns revenue — the founders do demos between product sprints. Two finalists: a 10-year enterprise AE (specialist, expensive) and a scrappy generalist who has done SDR, support, and ops at two startups.
choices: The generalist — at 6 people you need range: they can sell, onboard, and support while you learn what the sales motion actually is
Hire the AE part-time as an advisor and keep looking
The enterprise AE — revenue is the bottleneck, hire the proven closer
Neither — wait until you can afford both
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. At employee six you do not yet know your sales motion — hiring an expensive specialist optimizes a playbook you have not discovered. The generalist sells, learns, onboards, and supports, generating the data the future specialist will need. The AE (C) is the right hire at employee 25, not employee 6; waiting (D) leaves the bottleneck choked; part-time advisors (B) do not carry quotas.
scenarios.hint: Do you know your sales motion yet — or do you still need someone who can discover it while doing three other jobs?
objectives: Hire for the current stage, not the future org chart
Match hire cost to validated motion
evidence: no revenue owner; sales motion unknown

scenarios.title: Culture Violation by a Top Performer
scenarios.situation: Your best engineer — 3x the output of anyone else, critical to the roadmap — publicly berated a junior designer in Slack. Two team members have quietly asked about it. Your principles doc says 'disagree respectfully.'
choices: Move them to isolated work so the friction disappears
Nothing formal — their output justifies latitude, address it casually later
Fire them immediately to send a message

Address it directly and promptly: private conversation, clear that the behavior violates a stated principle regardless of output, specific consequences, and a visible (appropriate) follow-up to the team
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Tolerating the violation (B) rewrites your culture in front of everyone watching — principles that bend for top performers are posters, not culture. Immediate firing (C) skips proportionality and due process; isolation (A) avoids the leadership moment. The direct conversation upholds the standard while preserving the person if they correct — and the team's trust either way.
scenarios.hint: What does the rest of the team learn from what you do in the next 48 hours?
evidence: public berating in Slack, 2 team members raised it

scenarios.title: The Underperforming Early Hire
scenarios.situation: Employee #4 joined 14 months ago as a generalist and was heroic early. The company has outgrown the role: they now struggle with the specialized work, miss deadlines, and the team routes around them. They are loyal and well-liked.
choices: Keep them — loyalty matters and they will grow into it
Fire them this week — the team has already decided
Have an honest conversation: name the gap specifically, offer a 30-day improvement plan with measurable goals tied to the evolved role, and be prepared to part respectfully if it does not close
Quietly hire their replacement and let them figure it out
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Loyalty without performance is a slow tax the whole team pays — but surprise firings of early loyalists destroy trust. The honest path respects both: specific gap, real support, measurable bar, clear timeline. Keeping them (A) normalizes underperformance; immediate firing (B) betrays the early compact; stealth replacement (D) is cowardice the team will detect instantly.
scenarios.hint: What does the team learn if loyalty alone protects a struggling role — and what do they learn from an honest, supported process?
objectives: Give a real chance with a real bar
evidence: role evolved past their skills; team routing around them

scenarios.title: Equity for Employee Seven
scenarios.situation: You are offering employee #7, a senior engineer, a package. Your first engineer got 1.5%. Market data says 0.25-0.5% is now normal at your stage. The candidate asks for 1%, citing the first engineer's grant.
choices: Match the 1% — internal equity demands equal grants
Offer 0.4% with a clear explanation: grants reflect risk and stage at time of joining; earlier hires took more risk for more upside, and the philosophy is public and consistent
Refuse to discuss the first engineer's grant — compensation is confidential
Offer 1% but with a longer vesting schedule to compensate
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Equity compensates risk at time of joining — the first engineer bet on an unproven company; employee seven joins a funded, de-risked one. Equal grants (A) ignore this and inflate dilution; secrecy (C) breeds distrust when numbers inevitably leak; longer vesting (D) is a gimmick that complicates the standard. A published philosophy makes differentiated grants feel fair instead of arbitrary.
scenarios.hint: What is the equity actually paying for — the work, or the risk taken at the time of joining?
objectives: Price equity by risk at grant time
Publish the philosophy, differentiate the numbers
Treat transparency as the fairness mechanism

scenarios.title: The Co-Founder Conflict
scenarios.situation: You and your co-founder disagree fundamentally: they want to raise a big round and blitzscale; you want to grow profitably toward sustainability. Conversations are getting heated and the team senses the tension.
choices: Avoid the fight — table it until after the next milestone
You are CEO — decide unilaterally and expect commitment
Split the difference: raise a medium round and grow medium-fast
Structured decision process: agree on the decision criteria first (runway needs, market window, team capacity), gather the data both sides need, decide by a date — and commit publicly to the outcome
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. 'Disagree and commit' only works with a legitimate process: shared criteria, shared data, a deadline, and public commitment. Unilateral CEO fiat (B) on a strategy question poisons the partnership; splitting the difference (C) produces a strategy optimized for no one; tabling it (A) lets the tension metastasize while the team watches. Co-founder conflict is normal — unresolved process around it is fatal.
scenarios.hint: Is the disagreement about the strategy, or about not having a way to decide strategy?
objectives: Use criteria and data, not authority

scenarios.title: Remote-First Communication
scenarios.situation: Your 12-person team is remote across 6 time zones. Decisions are getting lost in Slack threads, two people built the same feature, and the 'quick sync' meetings are multiplying.
choices: Write it down: decisions live in docs with owner + deadline; async updates replace status meetings; Slack is for discussion, docs are for decisions
Hire a project manager to chase everyone
Move everyone to one time zone's working hours
More meetings — alignment requires face time, even virtual
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Remote dysfunction is a writing dysfunction: decisions trapped in ephemeral chat get rebuilt and re-litigated. Docs with owners and deadlines make decisions durable and discoverable across time zones; async written updates kill the status-meeting sprawl. More meetings (D) taxes the time zones hardest; a PM (B) adds process without fixing the medium; forced hours (C) destroys the hiring advantage of remote.
scenarios.hint: Where do your decisions live — in searchable docs, or in a Slack thread nobody can find next week?
objectives: Decisions live in docs, not chat
Fix the medium before adding process
evidence: lost decisions, duplicated work, meeting sprawl

scenarios.title: The Counteroffer
scenarios.situation: Your lead engineer — critical, underpaid relative to new offers — brings you a competing offer: 40% more cash at a late-stage startup. They say they would stay for a raise and a refresher grant. You can afford it, barely.
choices: Match it — losing them costs more than the raise
Let them go — matching counteroffers trains everyone to get competing offers
Match the substance but fix the system: retain them with adjusted comp, then audit everyone's comp against market and fix the philosophy that let a critical person drift 40% below market
Counter with equity only — preserve cash
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. The counteroffer is a symptom: your compensation system let a critical person drift 40% below market, which means others are drifting too. Retaining without fixing the system (A) buys one person and keeps the leak; never matching (B) is principled but loses someone you admit is critical; equity-only (D) ignores that cash was the gap. Fix the person and the system — that is the leadership move.
scenarios.hint: If one critical person is 40% below market, what does that tell you about everyone you have not heard from?
objectives: Fix the person and the philosophy
Audit comp before it becomes a crisis
evidence: critical, underpaid — system allowed the drift

scenarios.title: Letting Go With Dignity
scenarios.situation: You have decided to let go of a manager whose team has underperformed for two quarters despite a real PIP. The termination meeting is tomorrow. You are dreading it.
scenarios.prompt: What does a well-handled exit look like?
choices: Keep it to 3 minutes, security escort out, no team announcement — clean and fast

A private, direct 10-minute conversation: decision stated plainly, brief honest reason, generous logistics (severance, references, transition help) — then an honest, respectful team note within 24 hours
Give them another month — the PIP was harsh and the market is tough
Let HR handle it entirely so it stays professional
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Dignity and clarity are not opposites: plain language, honest reasons, and generous logistics respect the person while the prompt team note respects everyone else. The 3-minute escort (A) is humiliation theater; another month (C) re-litigates a decided PIP; outsourcing to HR (D) abdicates the leadership moment. The team will judge your culture by this meeting more than by any values doc.
scenarios.hint: What will the remaining team conclude about working here from how this exit is handled?
objectives: Be direct and humane in exits

domains.summary: Hiring, culture, and leading through scale.

scenarios.title: The Unsolicited Offer
scenarios.situation: A strategic acquirer — a company you have partnered with for a year — offers $45M cash for your $8M-ARR business growing 80% annually. No process, no other bidders, 30-day exclusivity requested. Your last round valued you at $40M.
choices: Neither accept nor reject: thank them, decline exclusivity for now, and quietly launch a targeted process with 4-6 logical buyers over 60 days — then decide with leverage
Accept but negotiate the earnout up instead of the price
Take it — $45M cash above the last valuation is a win, sign exclusivity
Reject it — 80% growth deserves a far higher multiple, hold out for $100M
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. An unsolicited offer is valuable information, not a verdict: it proves strategic interest exists, which is the raw material for a process. Signing exclusivity (C) surrenders your only leverage — competition. Rejecting outright (D) discards a real bird in hand for a hypothetical. The disciplined move converts one bidder's interest into a 60-day process, then decides with actual alternatives on the table.
scenarios.hint: Is this offer a verdict on your company's value, or the opening bid in a process you have not run yet?
objectives: Decide with alternatives, not in isolation

scenarios.title: Strategic vs Financial Buyer
scenarios.situation: Two bids: a strategic offers $60M (70% cash, 30% stock, 3-year founder vesting, big earnout); a PE firm offers $48M all-cash, no earnout, 18-month transition, clean close in 60 days.
choices: Reject both and keep growing — neither reflects the strategic value
Ask the strategic to match the PE terms at $60M
The strategic — $60M headline is $12M more, always take the higher number
The PE offer — $48M certain cash with clean terms likely beats $60M of contingent, handcuffed value once you risk-adjust the earnout and vesting
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Headline price is not take-home: the strategic's $60M includes an earnout you will likely under-earn (post-acquisition you control neither resources nor accounting), 30% buyer stock, and 3 years of golden handcuffs. Risk-adjusted, the $48M all-cash clean close is usually worth more — and 60 days of certainty beats 9 months of maybe. Taking the headline (C) is the classic founder error; (B) is worth attempting but rarely granted on all terms.
scenarios.hint: What is each offer worth in certain cash in your pocket within two years — not the headline?
objectives: Risk-adjust every term, not just price

scenarios.title: The Earnout Trap
scenarios.situation: The acquirer proposes: $30M cash at close plus $20M earnout if the product line hits $15M revenue in year one post-acquisition. You will report to their VP of Product, who controls roadmap and marketing spend.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle the earnout?
choices: Accept — $15M is achievable and $50M total is the right valuation

Counter with targets you control, measured your way (e.g., product shipped + team retained + your P&L authority), or convert the earnout to cash at a discount — never accept targets controlled by their VP
Accept but ask for monthly reporting so you can track progress
Walk away from the whole deal over the earnout
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Earnouts fail when the acquirer controls the inputs: their VP owns roadmap and spend, so your $15M target depends on decisions you do not make — most such earnouts underpay. The fix is structural: targets within your control, your measurement, your P&L authority — or take the discounted cash now. Monthly reporting (C) watches the trap without disarming it; walking away (D) over-negotiates a fixable term.
scenarios.hint: Who controls whether the earnout target gets hit — you, or their VP?
objectives: Never accept earnouts on others' inputs
Convert contingent value to certain cash
evidence: $20M on $15M yr-1 revenue, you report to their VP

scenarios.title: Diligence Data Room
scenarios.situation: You are 30 days from launching a sale process. Your 'data room' is a shared drive with 400 unsorted files, the cap table lives in a founder's spreadsheet, and two top customers do not know you are exploring a sale.
choices: Hire a banker and let them organize everything
Launch the process now — momentum matters more than paperwork
Clean the data room first (2 weeks), verify the cap table with counsel, brief your customer champions privately — then launch; a messy room invites price chips
Tell all customers immediately — transparency above all
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Diligence discovers everything — the only question is whether you present it organized or they discover it chaotic. A messy room does not just slow the process; it manufactures 'issues' that become price chips. Customer champions must hear it from you first, privately, or a buyer's surprise call becomes a negative reference. Launching messy (B) or outsourcing organization (A) both cede control of your own narrative.
scenarios.hint: When the buyer finds a problem, do you want it to be one you disclosed with context, or one they discovered in a 400-file mess?

scenarios.title: The Acqui-Hire Lowball
scenarios.situation: Growth stalled at $1.2M ARR, cash runs out in 5 months. A large tech company offers $6M total — structured as retention packages for the team, nearly nothing for common shareholders (including you). The team does not know yet.
choices: Take it — $6M and the team lands safely; common shareholders get nothing but that is startup life
Reject it — fight for a real valuation or shut down with dignity
Negotiate the structure first: push for a carve-out for common (founder + early employees), better team economics, and be transparent with the team before deciding — then decide with full information
Hide the offer from the team and keep fundraising
scenarios.why: The correct answer is C. Acqui-hire offers are negotiable on structure even when price is fixed: management carve-outs for common shareholders are standard asks, and team economics (who gets what retention) determine whether your people actually land well. Deciding without the team (A, D) betrays the people the deal is supposedly for; reflex rejection (B) discards the only lifeboat without testing whether it can be improved. Transparency plus negotiation, then decide.
scenarios.hint: Who is this deal actually for — and have you negotiated the parts that serve them?

scenarios.title: Founder Vesting in the Deal
scenarios.situation: The term sheet: $55M acquisition, your 20% becomes $11M — but vests over 4 years with a 1-year cliff, reporting to an SVP you have never met, in a role described as 'VP of Innovation.' You are burned out.
choices: More cash, same vesting — the money is what matters
Refuse any vesting — you built it, you are done
Nothing — $11M is $11M, sign it

Shorter vesting (2 years) or accelerated vesting on termination without cause, a defined role with real scope and a named manager, and a severance floor — because 4 years of golden handcuffs when burned out is a retention failure waiting to happen
scenarios.why: The correct answer is D. Four-year re-vesting when burned out predicts either misery or departure — and departure forfeits the unvested millions, which is exactly the acquirer's design. Negotiate the handcuffs: shorter vesting, single/double-trigger acceleration, a real role with a known manager, severance. Nothing (C) accepts a probable forfeiture; cash-only focus (A) ignores that the $11M is mostly contingent; refusing vesting (B) is a non-starter that kills the deal.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the $11M if you quit in month 14 — and is that the likely outcome given burnout?
objectives: Negotiate the handcuffs, not just the headline
Price in your own burnout honestly
evidence: $11M over 4yr vest, 1yr cliff, unknown SVP, vague role

scenarios.title: The Auction vs the Single Bidder
scenarios.situation: Your banker proposes a broad auction: 30 buyers contacted, 8 weeks, maximum competitive tension. Your corp-dev contact at the most logical acquirer says: 'Skip the circus — we'll pay fair value now, but we won't bid against 29 others.'
choices: The single-bidder deal — the logical acquirer pays the strategic premium anyway, and auctions leak to competitors and employees
A targeted process: 5-7 logical buyers, quiet and controlled, with the logical acquirer included — competition among the few who'd pay strategic value, without the circus
No process — wait for inbound interest
The broad auction — competition is the only reliable price discovery
scenarios.why: The correct answer is B. Broad auctions maximize leaks (employees, customers, competitors learn you are for sale) while the single bidder maximizes bluff-calling risk. The targeted process threads it: enough credible buyers for real tension, few enough for confidentiality, including the logical acquirer so their 'fair value' gets market-tested. Process design is leverage design.
scenarios.hint: What are you optimizing — maximum bidders, or maximum credible tension with minimum leakage?
objectives: Test 'fair value' claims against a market
evidence: logical acquirer: fair value now, no bidding war

scenarios.title: After the Wire Transfer
scenarios.situation: The deal closed: $38M, life-changing money. It is week three. You wake up with no company, no 60-hour weeks, and a vague plan to 'figure out what's next.' Old colleagues are scattering. You feel unmoored.
scenarios.prompt: What is the healthiest first move?
choices: Execute a structured 90 days: scheduled rest first, then 20 exploratory conversations across advising/investing/building, then commit to one vehicle — with wealth, tax, and estate planning running in parallel
Angel-invest the whole network's startups right away — stay in the game
Start the next company immediately — momentum is everything
Drift for a year — you earned it, rest indefinitely
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Post-exit drift destroys more founders than failure: structure converts the void into a decision process. Scheduled rest first (not indefinite drift), then deliberate exploration across the three vehicles, then commitment — while the unglamorous money work (tax, diversification, estate) happens in parallel. Immediate next-company (C) skips the learning the exit bought; indefinite drift (D) becomes a year; instant angel (B) deploys capital before strategy.
scenarios.hint: Is 'figure out what's next' a plan — or the absence of one?

lessons.title: Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track — Core concepts
concepts: Entrepreneurship is a discipline, not a personality trait: a teachable method for discovering valuable problems and building solutions under uncertainty. The method improves your cost per experiment and your odds; it does not remove risk.

The foundations audit comes before scale: finance (read statements, model cash, understand runway), marketing (know the customer, the channel, the message), operations (deliver at volume, at cost). Beloved prototypes with broken foundations scale losses.

Problem discovery precedes product: structured customer interviews establish whether a pain is real, frequent, expensive, and budgeted — code is the most expensive hypothesis test, conversation the cheapest.

The MVP discipline: the minimum viable product is the smallest thing that tests the riskiest assumption. Concierge, Wizard-of-Oz, and landing-page MVPs validate demand before engineering validates the build.

Unit economics are the verdict on the business model: LTV must exceed CAC (healthy: 3:1), payback periods must fit your cash, and contribution margin must survive scale. Growth on broken unit economics is just faster losses.

Fundraising literacy: valuation is one term among many — dilution, liquidation preference, option pool, board control, and protective provisions determine what founders actually keep. Price practitioner programs (equity, time, cash) against verified acceleration, not marketing.

example.walkthrough: Lifetime is the reciprocal of monthly churn (4 months at 25% churn); LTV is monthly contribution margin times lifetime. The scenario's startup prints LTV/CAC = 0.67 — BROKEN — which is the arithmetic behind the scenario's verdict: each customer destroys $20. Change churn to 8% and watch the verdict flip; that sensitivity is the whole strategy conversation.

pitfalls: Common trap: building before discovering. Months of engineering on an assumed problem is the most expensive possible way to learn the problem wasn't real — interview first.
Common trap: confusing revenue with unit economics. A month where revenue beats ad spend says nothing about whether each customer pays back their acquisition cost over their lifetime.
Common trap: negotiating valuation instead of the term sheet. Dilution, liquidation preference, and the option pool shuffle determine founder outcomes more than the headline pre-money number.
Common trap: treating programs and accelerators as ideology. Price every offer — equity, time, cash — against verified acceleration for your specific company, not demo-day footage.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Entrepreneurship move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow
Interview/exam power: when asked 'how does X work?', narrate the journey — 'it starts here, then...'. This demonstrates senior-level systems thinking

example.code:
TRIGGER event occurs
  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.
example.walkthrough: This is the 'jet engine cutaway' for your field: instead of memorizing isolated facts, you see the entire flow as a moving sequence. Practice narrating this journey out loud.

pitfalls: Memorizing terms without understanding the processes they participate in
Drawing architecture diagrams as boxes without showing the data flow between them
Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence
lessons.try_it: Pick any process in this course. Write out the full journey from trigger to outcome, naming every system touched.

See it as a journey: identify the trigger, follow each handoff, watch state change at every step
Every step depends on the previous — a failure at any point breaks the chain. Map these dependencies
Connect Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track to the broader Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track ecosystem — nothing operates in isolation

  3. Answer the scenarios (decision drills)
  4. Finish with the mock assessment (timed, exam-style)
example.walkthrough: This bootcamp mirrors how professionals actually learn: concept first, then hands-on, then judgment under pressure. Trust the sequence.

pitfalls: Skipping lessons and jumping straight to scenarios — the scenarios assume the lesson vocabulary.
Treating the terminal labs as optional — muscle memory is what survives exam pressure.
Rushing. Spaced, deliberate reps beat one marathon session.
lessons.try_it: Open the terminal now and type: echo ready — confirm you see your text echoed back.

lessons.title: Study Strategy for Entrepreneurship
concepts: Time-box your sessions: 50 minutes of focused work, 10 minutes off. Three focused sessions beat one exhausted six-hour grind.
Active recall beats re-reading: after each lesson, close it and explain the key idea out loud in your own words before moving on.
The entrepreneurship examination rewards pattern recognition. Every scenario you answer builds a mental library of 'I've seen this shape before.'
Track your weak domains explicitly. Revisit them with the systems-anatomy lens: trace the full flow, find where your mental model breaks.

example.code:
WEEKLY RHYTHM (example)
  Mon/Wed/Fri: 2 new domains (lessons + labs)
  Tue/Thu: scenario drills on prior domains
  Sat: timed mock assessment
  Sun: review misses, rebuild weak areas
example.walkthrough: Elite performers don't study more hours — they study with tighter feedback loops. Every wrong answer is a precise map of what to fix next.

pitfalls: Passive highlighting and re-reading — feels productive, builds nothing.
Avoiding timed practice until 'ready' — the clock is a skill, train it early.
Studying only strengths — comfort is the enemy of growth.
lessons.try_it: Write down your three weakest areas right now. You will re-test them at the end of this bootcamp.

lessons.title: Entrepreneurship: Field Overview
concepts: The big picture first: Entrepreneurship sits at the intersection of theory you must know and judgment you must demonstrate.
Employers and examiners test the same thing: can you reason from first principles when the situation is novel, not just recite facts?
Every domain in this bootcamp maps to a real capability: something you will actually do, decide, or explain on the job.
The capstone at the end proves you can integrate everything — that is the artifact you show, not just talk about.

example.code:
MAP OF THE TERRITORY
  Foundations → Core systems → Applied judgment → Capstone proof
  Each layer assumes the last. There are no shortcuts, only compounding.
example.walkthrough: Keep this map in mind as you work through domains. When a lesson feels abstract, ask: 'what real decision does this prepare me for?'

pitfalls: Treating domains as isolated trivia — they connect. Always ask how this domain touches the others.
Ignoring the 'why' behind procedures — procedures change, principles don't.
Waiting until the end to attempt the capstone — start scoping it now.
lessons.try_it: Skim the domain list for this bootcamp. Write one sentence for each: what real-world capability does it build?

lessons.title: How Assessment Works Here
concepts: Knowledge checks verify understanding before a lesson counts as complete — you prove it, then it counts. No click-through completions.
Scenarios are scored on judgment: the right answer with the right reasoning. Read every 'why' explanation even when you answer correctly.
The mock assessment is timed and cumulative. It draws on all domains — treat it as the real exam rehearsal.
Labs verify hands-on skill in the terminal. If a check fails, the hint tells you exactly what to fix — iterate until green.

example.code:
SCORING MODEL
  Lessons: completion requires passing the knowledge check
  Scenarios: attempts tracked, streaks build mastery
  Labs: all checks must pass
  Mock: scored like the real thing — this is your readiness signal
example.walkthrough: The system is designed so that 'complete' means 'can actually do it.' Respect the bar and it will carry you through the real assessment.

pitfalls: Gaming the knowledge check by guessing — it exists to protect you from false confidence.
Skipping lab hints — they are targeted coaching, not cheating.
Taking the mock once — take it repeatedly until your score stabilizes above target.
lessons.try_it: Answer this lesson's knowledge check, then run one terminal lab to feel the verification loop.

lessons.title: Capstone: Venture Build Sprint — Blueprint
concepts: Your capstone proves integrated capability: Take an idea from validation through financial model to investor-ready pitch: customer evidence, unit economics, and a 10-slide deck you'd defend.
Scope it in milestones, not monoliths. Each milestone is independently demonstrable — if you run out of time, you still have working pieces.
Document as you build. The artifact plus the write-up is what you show; either alone is half the value.
Build in public where appropriate: version control, clear commits, a README that explains the why, not just the what.

example.code:
CAPSTONE MILESTONES
  1. Validate the problem with 20 customer interviews
  2. Define the business model and unit economics
  3. Build the 3-year financial model
  4. Create the 10-slide pitch deck
  5. Deliver the pitch and handle Q&A
example.walkthrough: A capstone is graded on integration and judgment, not just completion. At each milestone ask: 'what decision did I make here, and why this way?'

pitfalls: Scope creep — freezing the milestone list on day one protects you.
Building without documenting — you will forget your own reasoning within days.
Perfectionism on milestone 1 — get all milestones to 'working' before polishing any to 'great.'
lessons.try_it: Write your milestone list now, with a definition of done for each.

lessons.title: Capstone: Build Log & Documentation
concepts: Keep a build log: date, what you attempted, what worked, what failed, what you learned. This becomes your documentation draft.
Your README needs five sections: what it is, why it matters, how to run it, architecture decisions, and what you'd do with more time.
Screenshots and terminal transcripts beat prose for proving hands-on work. Capture evidence as you go.
Anticipate the three hardest questions about your capstone and write the answers before anyone asks.

example.code:
README SKELETON
  # Title — one-line value proposition
  ## Why — the problem this solves
  ## Quickstart — commands to run it
  ## Architecture — decisions and trade-offs
  ## Next steps — honest limitations
example.walkthrough: Documentation written after the fact reads like fiction. The build log keeps it honest — and honesty about limitations reads as seniority.

pitfalls: README as an afterthought — start it on day one, even as stubs.
Hiding limitations — naming them with a plan reads as maturity.
No reproduction steps — if they can't run it, it doesn't exist.
lessons.try_it: Create your capstone repo/directory and write the README skeleton today.

lessons.title: Capstone: Demo & Defense
concepts: Prepare a 5-minute demo: the problem, your approach, the working result, one hard decision you made. Rehearse it out loud twice.
Defense prep: for every tool and choice in your capstone, be ready to answer 'why this instead of the alternative?'
Connect each capstone decision back to bootcamp domains — this shows integrated understanding, not isolated effort.
End your demo with honest next steps. 'Here's what I'd harden for production' is the strongest closing line.

example.code:
DEMO ARC (5 min)
  0:00 — The problem (30s)
  0:30 — Your approach (60s)
  1:30 — Live working demo (120s)
  3:30 — One hard decision + trade-off (45s)
  4:15 — Next steps for production (45s)
example.walkthrough: The demo is a performance. Rehearsal is what makes it look effortless — and effortlessness reads as mastery.

pitfalls: Demoing without a fallback — have screenshots/video if live fails.
Over-running time — a tight 5 minutes beats a rambling 15.
Memorizing a script — know the beats, speak naturally.
lessons.try_it: Do a timed 5-minute dry run of your demo this week, even if the build isn't finished.

lessons.title: Finding Problems Worth Solving
concepts: Great businesses start from painful, frequent, expensive problems — not from solutions looking for problems.
The problem interview: ask about past behavior and pain, never about your idea — 'tell me about the last time...' beats 'would you use...?'
Willingness to pay is the only validation that counts — everything else (likes, signups, compliments) is vanity until money moves.
Founder-problem fit: the best opportunities sit at the intersection of real pain and your unfair advantage in solving it.

example.code:
PROBLEM INTERVIEW SCRIPT
  'Tell me about the last time [problem] happened.'
  'What did you do about it?'
  'What did that cost you (time/money)?'
  'What have you tried? Why didn't it work?'
  Never mention your solution. Listen for pain, frequency, budget.
example.walkthrough: Do 20 problem interviews before building anything — the patterns in answers 15-20 are the real insight.

pitfalls: Solution-first building — 'if we build it' is the most expensive hypothesis.
Asking 'would you use this?' — hypothetical yeses are worthless.
Interviewing friends — politeness masquerades as validation.
lessons.try_it: Write your problem-interview script (5 questions, zero solution mentions).

lessons.title: The Mom Test Principles
concepts: Bad data comes from bad questions: compliments, fluff ('I love it!'), and future promises ('I'd totally pay') — all worthless.
Good questions ask about specifics in the past: what they did, what it cost, what they tried — behavior beats opinion.
The Mom Test rule: if your mom can lie to make you feel good, so can customers — design questions even she can't flatter through.
Segment by behavior, not demographics: 'people who paid for X last month' beats 'millennials interested in Y.'

example.code:
QUESTION AUTOPSY
  Bad: 'Do you think this is a good idea?' (flattery bait)
  Bad: 'Would you pay $50?' (hypothetical)
  Good: 'What did you last pay to solve this?' (behavior)
  Good: 'Can I watch you do it now?' (reality)
  Past behavior predicts; opinions don't.
example.walkthrough: Rewrite every validation question through the Mom Test before asking it.

pitfalls: Leading questions — 'don't you hate it when...' manufactures agreement.
Pitching disguised as research — the moment you pitch, learning stops.
Counting enthusiasts — excitement without budgets is entertainment.
lessons.try_it: Take your three validation questions. Rewrite each to pass the Mom Test.

lessons.title: Minimum Viable Testing
concepts: The concierge MVP: deliver the service manually first — learn what customers actually want before automating anything.
The Wizard of Oz: fake the backend, real frontend — customers experience the product while you operate it by hand behind the curtain.
Landing page tests: measure real intent (email + pre-order) not vanity traffic — but only with honest fulfillment plans.
One metric per test: each experiment answers one question — 'will they pay?' not 'do they like the colors too?'

example.code:
MVP LADDER (cheapest first)
  1. Problem interviews (free)
  2. Landing page + pre-order ($100)
  3. Concierge: manual delivery ($500)
  4. Wizard of Oz: fake backend ($2k)
  5. Single-feature product ($10k+)
  Climb only when the cheaper test passes.
example.walkthrough: Each rung costs 5-10× the last — earn the right to climb with evidence.

pitfalls: Building the full product as the 'MVP' — that's not minimum or viable to test.
Testing five things at once — confounded experiments teach nothing.
Skipping rungs — each rung's evidence justifies the next rung's cost.
