lessons.try_it: Design the cheapest test for your riskiest assumption. Price it under $200.

lessons.title: Pivot or Persevere
concepts: The pivot is a structured course correction: same vision, new strategy — not random flailing between ideas.
Pivot types: zoom-in (one feature becomes the product), customer segment, channel, technology, business model — name your pivot type.
Persevere criteria: improving leading metrics on a reasonable timeline — flat metrics after real effort signal pivot time.
The sunk-cost trap: past investment doesn't justify future investment — decide on forward evidence, not backward spending.

example.code:
PIVOT DECISION FRAME
  Leading metrics improving? → persevere, double down
  Flat after 3+ real experiments? → pivot (name the type)
  Declining despite effort? → pivot or shut down
  Never: continue from sunk cost alone.
example.walkthrough: Schedule the pivot-or-persevere review quarterly — calendar discipline beats emotional drift.

pitfalls: Vanity-metric perseverance — 'users love us' without revenue or retention.
Pivot-hopping — changing strategy monthly tests nothing.
Sunk-cost escalation — good money after bad, justified by pride.
lessons.try_it: Define your leading metrics and the pivot trigger values now, in writing.

lessons.title: Business Model Canvas
concepts: Nine blocks: value proposition, customer segments, channels, relationships, revenue streams, key resources, activities, partners, cost structure — one page, full logic.
Start with value proposition + segments: if you can't state the value for a specific someone in one sentence, the rest is decoration.
Revenue streams before cost structure: prove someone pays before optimizing what it costs — the order prevents beautiful bankruptcies.
The canvas is a hypothesis document: every block is an assumption to test, ranked by risk — test riskiest first.

example.code:
CANVAS IN ONE LINE PER BLOCK
  VP: 'We help [segment] achieve [outcome] without [pain].'
  Segments: beachhead first, then expansion.
  Channels: where the segment already buys.
  Revenue: how money flows, per unit.
  Costs: what the machine consumes.
  Fill VP+segments first; the rest follows.
example.walkthrough: A canvas filled in an hour beats a 40-page plan — speed of iteration is the advantage.

pitfalls: Filling all nine blocks equally — VP and segments carry 80% of the risk.
Treating the canvas as a plan — it's a hypothesis list; test it.
One canvas forever — revisit quarterly; businesses evolve.
lessons.try_it: Fill a one-page canvas for your idea. Mark the three riskiest assumptions.

lessons.title: Revenue Models Compared
concepts: Subscription: predictable, compounding — but churn is the silent killer; net revenue retention is the metric.
Transactional/marketplace: take-rate on volume — needs liquidity (enough buyers AND sellers) before the model works.
SaaS metrics: CAC, LTV, LTV:CAC ≥ 3, payback < 12 months — the unit-economics grammar investors speak.
Services/productized: high touch, high margin — productize delivery to escape the hours-for-dollars trap.

example.code:
MODEL MATH
  Subscription: 1000 × $50 × 12 = $600k ARR; 5% monthly churn → halve in ~13 months
  Marketplace: $1M GMV × 10% take = $100k revenue
  Services: $200/hr × 1000 hrs = $200k (capped by hours)
  The math reveals the model's nature.
example.walkthrough: Choose the model whose math matches your strengths — then learn its metrics cold.

pitfalls: Subscription without churn math — gross adds hide net decay.
Marketplace without liquidity plan — the chicken-and-egg kills most.
Services without productization — the founder becomes the bottleneck.
lessons.try_it: Model your idea three ways (subscription, transactional, services). Compare the math.

lessons.title: Unit Economics
concepts: Unit economics: the profit of one unit sold — if the unit loses money, scale multiplies losses.
CAC (customer acquisition cost): fully-loaded sales+marketing divided by new customers — the true price of growth.
LTV (lifetime value): gross margin × retention horizon — the prize; LTV:CAC ≥ 3 is the health threshold.
Contribution margin per unit must be positive before scaling — 'we'll make it up on volume' with negative margins is arithmetic suicide.

example.code:
UNIT CHECK
  Price: $100 | COGS: $30 → gross margin $70
  CAC: $50 → contribution $20 per customer
  LTV (3-yr): $70 × 3 = $210 → LTV:CAC = 4.2 ✓
  Payback: $50 / $70 per year ≈ 9 months ✓
  Healthy. Scale it.
example.walkthrough: Run the unit check before any growth spending — it's the go/no-go gate.

pitfalls: Blended CAC hiding channel rot — segment CAC by channel.
Ignoring payback period — LTV:CAC of 5 with 3-year payback still kills cash.
Negative contribution margin at scale — the fastest way to go broke.
lessons.try_it: Compute CAC, LTV, LTV:CAC, and payback for your model with honest numbers.

lessons.title: Pricing Strategy
concepts: Value-based pricing: price on the customer's outcome value, not your cost — cost-plus leaves money and positioning on the table.
Good-better-best: three tiers anchor the middle — most buyers choose middle; the top tier makes it look reasonable.
Freemium: free tier acquires, paid converts — the free tier must be valuable but incomplete; conversion rate is the metric.
Pricing is positioning: premium prices signal premium value — underpricing can reduce demand for status goods.

example.code:
PRICING LADDER
  Cost: $20/unit
  Cost-plus ($30): leaves value on table
  Competitor-matched ($45): commodity framing
  Value-based ($120): priced on $1000 outcome value
  Same product, 4× revenue — pricing is strategy.
example.walkthrough: Test pricing with real offers — surveys lie, A/B purchase tests don't.

pitfalls: Cost-plus default — the laziest pricing strategy.
Single tier — no anchor, no upsell path.
Set-and-forget — pricing is a lever; pull it deliberately.
lessons.try_it: Design good-better-best tiers for your offering with prices and feature splits.

lessons.title: Bootstrapping vs Raising
concepts: Bootstrapping: customer-funded growth — slower, but you keep control and the business must work from day one.
Venture: rocket fuel for winner-take-all markets — but it demands 10× outcomes and a credible path to them.
The fit test: raise when the market rewards speed over efficiency and the opportunity is large enough for fund economics; bootstrap otherwise.
Hybrid paths: bootstrap to traction, then raise from strength — the best terms come to companies that don't need the money.

example.code:
FUNDING FIT
  Bootstrap if: profitable niches, lifestyle goals, capital-efficient model
  Raise if: network effects, land-grab market, 10× potential
  Hybrid: bootstrap to $1M ARR, raise to scale
  Mismatch (raising for a lifestyle business) destroys both.
example.walkthrough: Choose funding by market physics, not prestige — the wrong capital is worse than none.

pitfalls: Raising for ego — venture is a tool, not a trophy.
Bootstrapping a land-grab — slow death against funded competitors.
No decision — drifting between modes gets neither's benefits.
lessons.try_it: Score your venture on the fit test. Write the verdict and reasons.

lessons.title: The Funding Ladder
concepts: Pre-seed: idea + team + early signals — friends, family, angels; $100k-$1M on narrative and trust.
Seed: product + initial traction — seed funds/angels; $1-4M to find repeatability.
Series A: repeatable growth engine — $5-15M to scale what works; the 'prove the machine' round.
Each round must buy the milestones that justify the next round's valuation — the ladder only works upward.

example.code:
ROUND → MUST PROVE
  Pre-seed → team + problem evidence
  Seed → product + early traction
  Series A → repeatable growth + unit economics
  Series B+ → market leadership + path to profit
  Raise for the next proof, not the current comfort.
example.walkthrough: Plan raises backward from the proof each round must deliver.

pitfalls: Raising without the proof for the next round — the ladder breaks.
Over-raising early — dilution and expectations you can't meet.
Under-raising — dying 80% to the milestone is the worst outcome.
lessons.try_it: Map your next 18 months: what proof justifies what round at what valuation?

lessons.title: Term Sheets Decoded
concepts: Valuation (pre/post): the headline number — but terms matter more than the number for founder outcomes.
Liquidation preference: 1× non-participating is standard; participating preferred or multiples quietly transfer outcomes to investors.
Pro-rata and anti-dilution: who gets to maintain ownership and who gets protected in down rounds — read both carefully.
Control provisions: board seats, protective provisions, vesting — the governance that outlives the honeymoon.

example.code:
TERM RED FLAGS
  🚩 Participating preferred (double-dip)
  🚩 >1× liquidation multiple
  🚩 Full-ratchet anti-dilution
  🚩 Investor majority board control
  🚩 4-yr vesting with no founder acceleration
  Green: 1× non-participating, broad-based weighted average.
example.walkthrough: Get a startup lawyer before signing anything — the most expensive legal fees are the ones you skip.

pitfalls: Optimizing valuation over terms — a high valuation with bad terms loses.
Skipping counsel — template understanding isn't legal advice.
Ignoring control — economics without governance is a passenger seat.
lessons.try_it: Take a sample term sheet. Flag every non-standard term with its consequence.

lessons.title: Financial Modeling
concepts: The model is a thinking tool, not a prediction: it forces explicit assumptions about growth, margins, and cash.
Build drivers, not lines: revenue = customers × ARPA, not 'revenue grows 10%' — drivers connect to actions.
Cash is the constraint: runway = cash / burn — the model must show the cash-out date under multiple scenarios.
Scenario planning: base, upside, downside — the downside case with 6+ months buffer is the operating plan.

example.code:
MODEL SKELETON
  Drivers: leads → conversion → customers → ARPA
  Costs: COGS, headcount, fixed
  Cash: starting + inflows − outflows = runway
  Scenarios: base / upside / downside
  Every number traces to a driver assumption.
example.walkthrough: If you can't explain every driver assumption in one sentence, the model is fiction.

pitfalls: Top-down fantasy — '1% of a billion' isn't a driver.
Single scenario — the base case is never what happens.
Ignoring cash timing — profitable on paper, dead from payroll timing.
lessons.try_it: Build the driver skeleton for your venture: 5 drivers, 3 scenarios.

lessons.title: Positioning and Messaging
concepts: Positioning is the mental slot you own: 'the X for Y' — without it, you're compared on price alone.
The positioning statement: for [target], who [need], our [category] provides [benefit] unlike [alternative] — fill it precisely.
Messaging hierarchy: tagline (memory), value props (reasons), proof points (evidence) — each level supports the one above.
Repositioning the competition: define them before they define you — 'the old way' framing makes you the future.

example.code:
POSITIONING WORKSHOP
  For: remote teams drowning in meetings
  Who need: decisions without calls
  Our async platform: resolves threads in hours
  Unlike: Slack chaos and Zoom fatigue
  Slot owned: 'decisions without meetings.'
example.walkthrough: If you can't state your positioning in one sentence, the market will position you — usually as 'expensive' or 'complicated.'

pitfalls: Feature-list positioning — features don't occupy mental slots; outcomes do.
Positioning for everyone — a slot for everyone is a slot for no one.
Set-and-forget — reposition as markets shift.
lessons.try_it: Write your one-sentence positioning. Test it on five people; iterate until they repeat it back.

lessons.title: Acquisition Channels
concepts: Channels are not interchangeable: each has different economics, intent levels, and scaling properties — match channel to model.
Search intent (SEO/SEM): captures existing demand — high intent, competitive, compounds (SEO) or rents (SEM).
Outbound (cold email/ads): creates demand — works for high-ACV B2B with tight ICP; spray-and-pray burns domains and brands.
Content/community: slow then compounding — the only channel that builds a durable asset; measure in quarters, not weeks.

example.code:
CHANNEL FIT MATRIX
  High ACV B2B → outbound + ABM
  Self-serve SaaS → SEO + content + PLG
  Local services → search + reviews
  Consumer → social + influencers + viral loops
  Wrong channel = right product, no customers.
example.walkthrough: Test channels in parallel small bets, then double down on the winner — don't marry a channel before dating several.

pitfalls: One-channel dependence — algorithm changes kill single-channel businesses.
Channel-model mismatch — enterprise outbound for $10/mo products.
Quitting content at month 2 — compounding starts around month 6.
lessons.try_it: Score 5 channels on fit for your model. Run $500 tests on the top 2.

lessons.title: Conversion Optimization
concepts: Conversion is a funnel: visitor → signup → activation → retention → revenue — find the leakiest stage and fix it first.
Activation is the money stage: the moment users experience core value — optimize time-to-value ruthlessly.
A/B testing discipline: one variable, sufficient sample, pre-registered hypothesis — otherwise it's decoration.
Friction audit: every field, click, and wait step costs conversion — remove, don't decorate.

example.code:
FUNNEL AUTOPSY
  10,000 visitors → 500 signups (5%) → 50 activated (10%) → 10 paid (20%)
  Leakiest: signup→activation (90% loss)
  Fix: onboarding email sequence + in-app checklist
  Result: activation 10%→25% = 2.5× revenue, zero new traffic.
example.walkthrough: Fix the leakiest stage first — a 2× improvement at the worst stage beats 10% everywhere.

pitfalls: Redesigning the homepage first — the leak is usually deeper in the funnel.
Testing without hypotheses — change bingo, not optimization.
Ignoring activation — signups that never activate are vanity.
lessons.try_it: Map your funnel with real numbers. Circle the leakiest stage and one fix.

lessons.title: Retention and Expansion
concepts: Retention is the growth engine: 5% churn improvement compounds harder than 5% acquisition improvement — the math is exponential.
Onboarding defines retention: users who reach the aha-moment in session one retain at 3× the rate of those who don't.
Expansion revenue (upsell/cross-sell) is the best revenue — NRR > 100% means growth without new logos.
Churn forensics: exit interviews and usage-pattern analysis reveal whether churn is product, expectation, or fit — each needs different fixes.

example.code:
RETENTION LEVERS
  Onboarding: time-to-value < 1 session
  Habits: core action frequency (weekly active)
  Expansion: land-and-expand paths built in
  Save plays: at-risk triggers + human outreach
  Measure: NRR, logo retention, cohort curves.
example.walkthrough: Cohort curves don't lie: flattening curves = product-market fit; declining curves = a leaky bucket with marketing.

pitfalls: Acquisition-only growth — the treadmill that never ends.
Averaging churn — segment by cohort; averages hide the story.
No save plays — at-risk users need intervention, not emails.
lessons.try_it: Plot one cohort curve from your data (or hypothetical). Is it flattening or declining?

lessons.title: Discovery Selling
concepts: Discovery before pitch: understand the prospect's pain, process, and power structure before presenting anything.
The 70/30 rule: prospect talks 70% — your questions do the selling; premature pitching triggers resistance.
Budget, authority, need, timeline (BANT): qualify ruthlessly — unqualified pipeline is fiction.
Next steps always: every interaction ends with a dated commitment — 'let me think' is a polite no.

example.code:
DISCOVERY QUESTIONS
  'Walk me through how you handle X today.'
  'What does that cost you when it breaks?'
  'Who else weighs in on this decision?'
  'What happens if nothing changes?'
  Pain → cost → power → urgency.
example.walkthrough: Discovery is diagnosis — prescription without diagnosis is malpractice.

pitfalls: Pitching in the first 5 minutes — you haven't earned the right.
Skipping BANT — hope is not a qualification method.
No next step — the deal dies in 'thinking about it.'
lessons.try_it: Write 5 discovery questions for your product. No pitching allowed.

lessons.title: Demos That Close
concepts: Demo the prospect's use case, not your feature list — 'here's your Tuesday morning' beats 'here are 40 features.'
The 3-act demo: their pain (mirror it), your solution (show the fix), their future (paint the outcome).
Check-ins, not monologues: 'does this match how you work?' every 3 minutes — silent audiences aren't sold.
End with the trial close: 'if we could do X, would you move forward?' — test temperature before proposing.

example.code:
DEMO FLOW
  0:00 'Show me your current process' (their world)
  5:00 'Here's where the pain hits' (mirror)
  10:00 'Watch it disappear' (your fix, their data)
  20:00 'Your team next quarter' (future paint)
  25:00 Trial close
  Their story, your tool.
example.walkthrough: The best demo feels like the prospect discovered the solution themselves.

pitfalls: Feature tours — nobody buys features; they buy outcomes.
No check-ins — silence isn't agreement.
Skipping the trial close — proposing to a cold room.
lessons.try_it: Outline a 25-minute demo for your product using the 3-act flow.

lessons.title: Objection Handling
concepts: Objections are buying signals in disguise: 'it's too expensive' means 'convince me of value' — engage, don't evade.
The LAER method: Listen, Acknowledge, Explore, Respond — diagnose before prescribing.
Price objections are value objections: reframe to cost-of-inaction and ROI — never discount first; discounting trains price focus.
Preempt the top 3 objections in your materials — handling them before they're raised is inoculation.

example.code:
LAER IN ACTION
  'It's too expensive.'
  Listen: (full stop, no interrupt)
  Acknowledge: 'Price matters — let's make sure the math works.'
  Explore: 'What are you comparing it to?'
  Respond: ROI math, not apology.
  Diagnose, then prescribe.
example.walkthrough: Welcome objections — silence is worse; objections tell you what to solve.

pitfalls: Discounting first — trains the market to wait for discounts.
Arguing — the prospect is always right about their concerns.
Ignoring objections — unhandled objections kill deals silently.
lessons.try_it: Write LAER responses to your top 3 objections.

lessons.title: Closing and Follow-Up
concepts: Assume the close: 'shall we start with 10 seats?' beats 'would you like to buy?' — presumptive closes test readiness.
The takeaway close: 'it sounds like this might not be the right fit' — reverses pressure and surfaces real objections.
Follow-up sequences: 80% of sales need 5+ touches — most reps quit at 2; systematize persistence.
CRM discipline: every interaction logged, next step dated — pipeline hygiene is revenue hygiene.

example.code:
FOLLOW-UP CADENCE
  Day 1: thank-you + summary + next step
  Day 3: value-add (relevant insight)
  Day 7: check-in with new angle
  Day 14: break-up email ('should I close this?')
  80% need 5+ touches. Automate the sequence.
example.walkthrough: The fortune is in the follow-up — systematically, not hopefully.

pitfalls: One-and-done outreach — the data says 5+ touches.
No CRM hygiene — unlogged pipeline is imaginary pipeline.
Weak closes — 'let me know' isn't a close.
lessons.try_it: Write your 4-touch follow-up sequence with dates and angles.

lessons.title: Entity and Structure
concepts: LLC vs C-corp: LLCs for lifestyle/small businesses (pass-through, simple); C-corps for venture-scale (investor-required, Delaware standard).
Delaware C-corp is the venture default — investors, option pools, and acquisition mechanics all assume it.
Founder vesting with cliff: 4-year vest, 1-year cliff — protects the company when co-founders leave early.
83(b) elections: file within 30 days of restricted stock grants — missing it creates catastrophic tax bills.

example.code:
FORMATION CHECKLIST
  ☐ Entity chosen for funding path
  ☐ Delaware C-corp if raising venture
  ☐ Founder vesting + cliff in place
  ☐ 83(b) filed within 30 days
  ☐ Cap table maintained from day one
  Get counsel; this is not DIY territory.
example.walkthrough: Formation mistakes compound for the company's entire life — get it right at birth.

pitfalls: Wrong entity for the path — converting later is expensive.
No vesting — the departed co-founder owns 40% forever.
Missed 83(b) — the 30-day window never reopens.
lessons.try_it: For your venture: entity choice, vesting terms, and 83(b) status — write the answers.

lessons.title: Contracts That Matter
concepts: Customer contracts: scope, payment terms, IP ownership, limitation of liability, termination — the five clauses that prevent 90% of disputes.
Contractor agreements: work-for-hire + IP assignment + confidentiality — without them, contractors may own what you paid for.
Founder agreements: roles, vesting, IP assignment, dispute resolution — the prenup every founding team needs.
Never sign without reading: the 'standard' contract from the other side is standard for them.

example.code:
CONTRACT SCAN (5 min)
  1. Parties and scope — what's actually covered?
  2. Money — amounts, timing, late terms?
  3. IP — who owns what?
  4. Liability — caps and exclusions?
  5. Exit — termination and post-term?
  Five clauses, five minutes, most disputes prevented.
example.walkthrough: The contract you don't read is the dispute you fund later.

pitfalls: Verbal agreements — 'we agreed' without writing is a future lawsuit.
No IP assignment — paying for work you don't own.
Ignoring liability caps — unlimited liability for limited upside.
lessons.try_it: Pull your most important unsigned agreement. Run the 5-minute scan.

lessons.title: Hiring Your First Team
concepts: Hire for the bottleneck: the constraint that, relieved, unlocks growth — not the role that seems prestigious.
The first 10 hires define the culture: optimize for slope (trajectory) over y-intercept (current skill) — learners beat knowers early.
Contractors before employees: validate the role's value with contractors before committing to headcount.
Fire fast on values, coach on skills: culture violations don't improve; skill gaps sometimes do.

example.code:
HIRING SEQUENCE
  1. Name the bottleneck (one)
  2. Contractor to validate (3 months)
  3. Hire for slope + values fit
  4. 30-60-90 plan with clear outcomes
  5. Weekly feedback, no surprises
  Each hire is a hypothesis — test it.
example.walkthrough: Early hires are leverage or drag — there is no neutral.

pitfalls: Hiring for prestige — titles don't relieve bottlenecks.
Slow firing on values — culture rot compounds.
No 30-60-90 — undefined success is unachievable success.
lessons.try_it: Name your current bottleneck role. Contractor or hire — and why?

lessons.title: Operational Systems
concepts: The business runs on systems, not heroics: documented processes for sales, delivery, finance, and support — the founder's job is building the machine.
Financial hygiene: separate accounts, monthly closes, 13-week cash forecast — the visibility that prevents surprises.
Tool stack minimalism: one tool per job, integrated — tool sprawl is process debt.
The vacation test: if the business breaks when you leave for two weeks, you have a job, not a company.

example.code:
SYSTEMS AUDIT
  ☐ Sales process documented?
  ☐ Delivery checklist exists?
  ☐ Monthly close < 10 days?
  ☐ 13-week cash forecast current?
  ☐ Can you take 2 weeks off?
  No to any = the bottleneck is you.
example.walkthrough: Build systems that survive your absence — that's the actual company.

pitfalls: Heroics as strategy — unsustainable and unscalable.
No financial visibility — surprises are always bad.
Tool sprawl — five tools doing one job's work.
lessons.try_it: Run the systems audit on your venture. Fix the worst 'no' this week.

lessons.title: The Founder's Mindset: Risk, Ambiguity, and Ownership
concepts: Founders trade a predictable salary for equity in an uncertain outcome. The job is making high-stakes decisions with incomplete information, over and over, for years.
Ambiguity tolerance is the core skill: markets shift, early data is thin, and waiting for certainty almost always means moving too late.
Ownership means the buck stops with you — angry customers, missed payroll, failed launches all land on the founder's desk with no one to escalate to.
Resilience is a system, not a trait. Build support structures — a co-founder, mentors, health routines — because raw motivation alone will not survive year two.

example.code:
FOUNDER READINESS AUDIT
  1. Can I survive 18 months with no salary? (runway, not hope)
  2. Who gives me hard truths when I am wrong? (name them)
  3. What is my kill criterion — the signal I will shut this down?
  4. What weekly routine protects my judgment? (sleep, exercise, review)
example.walkthrough: Run this audit honestly before incorporating. A founder who cannot answer question 3 will ride a dead idea for two extra years — the most expensive failure mode in startups.

pitfalls: Romanticizing the founder lifestyle — the job is mostly unglamorous problem-solving under pressure.
Confusing confidence with evidence — conviction must be earned through customer contact, not asserted.
Going it alone when you need a sparring partner — isolation degrades judgment faster than anything else.
lessons.try_it: Complete the four-question Founder Readiness Audit in writing. Share it with one person who will tell you the truth.

lessons.title: Founder Roles and the Co-Founder Question
concepts: Solo founders keep full control and move fast, but carry every burden alone and present higher risk to investors who fear the 'bus factor'.
Co-founders split the load and bring complementary skills, but a bad co-founder relationship is the number one cause of early startup death — worse than no co-founder at all.
The classic split is builder (product/technology) plus seller (customers/revenue), with a third chair for domain expertise when the industry demands it.
Vesting protects everyone: four-year vesting with a one-year cliff is the standard because it aligns commitment and lets the company recover equity if someone leaves early.

example.code:
CO-FOUNDER FIT CHECKLIST
  Skills: complementary, overlapping enough to communicate
  Values: aligned on ambition, ethics, and work intensity
  Conflict style: can we fight productively? (test on a hard decision)
  Commitment: equal financial runway and time availability
  Paperwork: vesting schedule + IP assignment BEFORE real work starts
example.walkthrough: Do not skip the conflict-style test. Ask your prospective co-founder to disagree with you about something real and watch how they handle it — that preview is the partnership.

pitfalls: Splitting equity 50/50 by default — equity should reflect contribution, risk, and role, decided deliberately.
Skipping vesting 'because we trust each other' — trust is why vesting exists; it is insurance, not insult.
Choosing a co-founder for comfort — choose for complementary capability and productive friction.
lessons.try_it: Score one real or hypothetical co-founder candidate against the five checklist rows. Write down the weakest row and how you would address it.

lessons.title: The First 90 Days: From Zero to Operating Company
concepts: Days 1-30 are for evidence, not incorporation: run customer interviews, test willingness to pay, and kill weak ideas before spending a dollar on legal structure.
The minimum viable company is boring on purpose — entity formed, EIN obtained, business bank account opened, basic bookkeeping running. Glamour comes later.
Your first metrics are learning metrics: interviews completed, experiments run, signups from landing pages. Revenue metrics come after you have something people want.
Set a weekly operating rhythm from day one: a written plan, a review of what was learned, and one decision that moves the riskiest assumption forward.

example.code:
90-DAY LAUNCH PLAN
  Days 1-30: VALIDATE — 25 customer interviews, problem + willingness-to-pay evidence
  Days 31-60: BUILD — minimum viable product/test, first 10 users, feedback loop
  Days 61-90: OPERATE — entity + banking + books, pricing test, first revenue or LOIs
  Weekly: 60-minute review — what did we learn, what dies, what is next
example.walkthrough: The 90-day plan forces a cadence most founders never establish. Week 12 arrives whether you planned or not — this makes sure it arrives with evidence.

pitfalls: Incorporating on day one — structure follows evidence, not the other way around.
Building before talking to customers — the 90-day plan bans this for the first 30 days.
No weekly review — without it, you will mistake motion for progress.
lessons.try_it: Draft your own 90-day plan against the template above, replacing the generic milestones with your idea's riskiest assumptions.

lessons.title: The Business as a Living Flow
concepts: A business is not an org chart — it is a flow: acquisition brings strangers in, activation turns them into users, revenue turns users into money, operations turns money into capacity.
Each stage feeds the next, and the output of operations (product quality, support capacity, cash) feeds back into acquisition. Break any link and the whole system starves.
Money is the system's blood: revenue funds operations, operations improve the product, the product improves acquisition. Trace every dollar through this loop before spending it.
New founders obsess over single stages (more ads! more features!). Systems thinkers watch the interfaces between stages — that is where companies actually die.

example.code:
THE FOUR-STAGE FLOW
  ACQUIRE: strangers discover you (marketing, referrals, sales)
    -> ACTIVATE: they experience value (onboarding, first win)
    -> REVENUE: value converts to money (pricing, upsell, retention)
    -> OPERATE: money becomes capacity (team, systems, product)
  FEEDBACK: operations quality -> acquisition efficiency (reputation, referrals)
example.walkthrough: Map your own venture onto this flow tonight. For each arrow between stages, write the conversion rate — the arrows with no number are where your ignorance lives.

pitfalls: Optimizing one stage in isolation — doubling acquisition with broken activation just doubles churn.
Ignoring feedback delays — operational improvements take quarters to show up in acquisition; impatience kills good investments.
Treating the flow as linear — it is a loop. Neglect the return path and growth becomes a treadmill.
lessons.try_it: Draw the four-stage flow for a business you know well. Label each arrow with what flows across it and one metric that measures it.

lessons.title: Bottlenecks and Leverage Points
concepts: Every system has exactly one binding constraint at a time: the bottleneck that caps total throughput no matter how much you improve everything else.
Finding the bottleneck is a measurement problem, not an opinion problem — follow the queue. Where do leads pile up? Where do customers wait? That pile is the constraint.
Leverage points are the opposite: small changes with outsized effects. A 10% pricing change beats a 10% traffic change because it flows straight to margin.
Constraints move. Fix the sales bottleneck and fulfillment becomes the constraint. Systems leadership is the permanent hunt for the next bottleneck.

example.code:
BOTTLENECK HUNT (weekly)
  1. List each stage's throughput (leads, activations, purchases, deliveries)
  2. Find the lowest number — that is your constraint
  3. Put 80% of improvement effort on that one stage
  4. Re-measure next week: did the constraint move?
  5. Never optimize a non-constraint — it is theater
example.walkthrough: Run the bottleneck hunt on your venture weekly. Most founders spread effort evenly across stages — which means they are mostly polishing non-constraints.

pitfalls: Fixing what is easy instead of what constrains — comfort work feels productive and changes nothing.
Adding capacity before the bottleneck — more ad spend into a broken funnel is just expensive churn.
Declaring victory permanently — the constraint always moves; the hunt never ends.
lessons.try_it: Pick a real or hypothetical business. Invent plausible stage throughputs, identify the constraint, and write the one improvement you would fund this week.

lessons.title: The Story Arc: Problem, Shift, Future
concepts: Every great pitch is a story in three acts: the world has a painful problem, something shifted that makes the old answer obsolete, and your company is the future arriving early.
Open with the customer, not the company. 'Dentists lose $40k a year to no-shows' beats 'We are an AI scheduling platform' — pain first, technology second.
The 'shift' is your why-now: a regulation changed, a technology got cheap, behavior moved. Without a shift, investors hear 'why hasn't this been built already?'
End the arc on inevitability: given the problem and the shift, your company is the obvious winner. Investors fund futures they can already see.

example.code:
STORY ARC TEMPLATE
  ACT 1 — PROBLEM: [customer] loses [money/time] because [broken status quo]
  ACT 2 — SHIFT: [technology/regulation/behavior] changed, so the old fix no longer works
  ACT 3 — FUTURE: We are [company]; we [solution], and here is the proof: [traction]
  CLOSE: This market is [$X] and we will own [wedge]
example.walkthrough: Write your arc in 60 seconds of spoken words before touching slides. If you cannot say it, no deck design will save it — the story is the pitch, the deck is the prop.

pitfalls: Leading with features — investors buy outcomes and inevitability, not feature lists.
Skipping the why-now — without a shift, your pitch sounds like a solution in search of a problem.
Making yourself the hero — the customer is the hero; you are the guide with the plan.
lessons.try_it: Write your three-act arc for your venture in under 100 words. Time yourself reading it aloud — target 60 seconds.

lessons.title: Deck Architecture: The Ten Slides That Matter
concepts: The standard ten: problem, solution, why now, market, product, traction, business model, team, financials, ask. Every investor has seen this order — deviating without reason creates friction.
One idea per slide, one headline that carries the message. If a slide needs you to explain it, the slide failed — redesign until the headline alone persuades.
Traction is the hinge slide: everything before it is a claim, everything after is a plan. Put your strongest proof here and spend the most rehearsal time on it.
The appendix is your armor: detailed financials, technical deep-dives, customer logos. You never present it — you deploy it when questions come.

example.code:
TEN-SLIDE SKELETON
  1. Problem (pain, with numbers)      2. Solution (your answer, simply)
  3. Why now (the shift)             4. Market (size + wedge)
  5. Product (show, minimal text)    6. TRACTION (proof — the hinge)
  7. Business model (how money flows) 8. Team (why you win)
  9. Financials (3-year shape)       10. Ask (amount, use, milestones)
  APPENDIX: everything a skeptic could ask
example.walkthrough: Build the skeleton with headlines only — no design yet. If the ten headlines read as a persuasive paragraph, the architecture works; design is just clothing.

pitfalls: Twenty-slide decks — length signals you cannot prioritize; ten forces choices.
Text walls — if they are reading, they are not listening. Headline plus visual, nothing more.
Burying traction on slide 8 — your proof belongs at the hinge, slide 6, where attention peaks.
lessons.try_it: Write the ten headlines for your deck. Read them in sequence — does the paragraph persuade a stranger? Revise until it does.

lessons.title: The Traction Slide: Proof Before Promises
concepts: Traction is evidence that the future you describe is already arriving: revenue, users, retention, LOIs, pilots — ordered by how hard each is to fake.
Revenue beats users, retention beats signups, paid pilots beat LOIs, LOIs beat 'interest'. Rank your proof honestly and lead with the strongest tier you truly have.
Growth rate matters more than absolute numbers: $10k MRR growing 20% monthly is more exciting than $50k flat. Show the curve, not just the point.

Pre-revenue founders still have traction options: waitlist conversion rates, paid deposits, letters of intent, usage data from an MVP. 'No traction' is a choice to present nothing — present your best evidence tier.

example.code:
TRACTION LADDER (lead with your highest true rung)
  $$ Revenue + growth rate + retention
  $$ Paid pilots / deposits
  $$ LOIs + waitlist with conversion data
  $$ MVP usage: DAU/WAU, engagement depth
  $$ Customer interviews: N completed, % with willingness to pay
  NEVER: vanity metrics alone (downloads, page views) as the headline
example.walkthrough: Audit your traction against the ladder. If your headline metric is two rungs below what you actually have, you are underselling — move the strongest real evidence to the top.

pitfalls: Vanity-metric headlines — investors discount downloads and views to zero; lead with money or retention.
Hiding flat numbers — show the curve honestly; a flat line with a credible plan beats a doctored one that collapses in diligence.
No proof tier at all — even 20 paid deposits beat a slide that says 'huge opportunity'.
lessons.try_it: Rank every traction metric you have on the ladder. Rewrite your traction slide headline around the highest true rung.

lessons.title: Financial Slides: Honest Projections
concepts: Investors know your projections are wrong — they are testing your thinking, not your prophecy. Show the drivers: customers × price × retention, not just the totals.
The three numbers that matter: burn rate (monthly spend), runway (months until money runs out), and the milestone this raise buys. Everything else is commentary.
Bottom-up beats top-down: 'we will capture 1% of a $10B market' is fantasy; '500 customers at $200/month with 5% monthly growth' is a model someone can interrogate.
Show the use of funds as milestones, not line items: '$500k buys 18 months and three proof points' — investors fund progress toward the next valuation inflection.

example.code:
FINANCIAL SLIDE ANATOMY
  Today: MRR/ARR, burn, runway, headcount
  Model: customers × ARPU × retention → 3-year revenue shape
  Unit economics: CAC, LTV, payback (from your analytics work)
  The ask: $X → 18 months → milestones A, B, C → next round at $Y valuation
example.walkthrough: Rebuild your financial slide bottom-up from unit economics. If the 3-year number cannot be derived from customers × price × retention, it is decoration — replace it with math.

pitfalls: Top-down market-share fantasy — '1% of $10B' has killed more pitches than any other sentence.
Hiding burn and runway — investors will ask; volunteering them signals operator maturity.
Precision theater — five-decimal projections scream amateur; round numbers and show drivers.
lessons.try_it: Recompute your 3-year revenue from customers × ARPU × retention on one page. Note where the model is most sensitive — that is what Q&A will attack.

lessons.title: Q&A and the Follow-Up Machine
concepts: Q&A is the real pitch: slides are monologue, questions are dialogue, and investors decide in dialogue. Rehearse answers to the 20 hardest questions, not just the deck.
The three-part answer: direct answer first ('yes, churn is 4%'), then context ('down from 9% after we fixed onboarding'), then the forward look ('targeting 2% by Q3'). Never bury the answer.
'I don't know, but I'll find out by Friday' beats a bluff every time — bluffs are remembered, honesty is respected, and Friday follow-ups are relationship gold.
The follow-up machine: every meeting ends with a next step and a date; every promise becomes a same-week email; every 'no' gets a quarterly update until it becomes a yes or a clear never.

example.code:
Q&A ARMOR (rehearse these cold)
  Why won't [incumbent] crush you? → wedge + speed + focus
  What if growth stalls? → leading indicators we watch + levers
  Why are you the team? → unfair advantage, not resumes
  What is the biggest risk? → name it, show the mitigation
  FOLLOW-UP CADENCE: thank-you (24h) → promised data (1wk) → monthly update → ask
example.walkthrough: Run a hostile mock Q&A with a friend playing the skeptic. Record it. The questions that made you flinch are your real homework — fix the business or fix the answer, but do not walk in unrehearsed.

pitfalls: Bluffing through unknowns — one caught bluff poisons the whole relationship.
Ending meetings without a next step — 'we'll be in touch' is how deals die quietly.
Going dark after a no — today's no is next year's yes if the updates keep coming.
lessons.try_it: List your 10 hardest questions and draft three-part answers for each. Schedule one hostile mock Q&A this week.

lessons.title: Unit Economics: CAC, LTV, and Payback
concepts: Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) is fully-loaded spend divided by new customers acquired — include salaries, tools, and overhead, not just ad spend, or the number lies.
Lifetime Value (LTV) is gross margin per customer times expected lifetime: for subscriptions, ARPU × gross margin ÷ churn rate. A 3:1 LTV:CAC ratio is the classic health threshold.
Payback period — months to recover CAC — is the constraint that kills: great ratios mean nothing if payback is 24 months and you have 12 months of runway.
Segment every ratio by channel and cohort. Blended unit economics hide the truth: one great channel subsidizing three terrible ones is not a business, it is an accident.

example.code:
UNIT ECONOMICS WORKUP
  CAC = total sales+marketing spend / new customers (fully loaded)
  LTV = ARPU × gross margin % / monthly churn %
  Payback = CAC / (ARPU × gross margin %)  → months
  HEALTH CHECK: LTV:CAC ≥ 3:1 AND payback < 12 months
  Example: $50 ARPU, 80% margin, 5% churn → LTV $800; CAC $200 → 4:1, 5-month payback ✓
example.walkthrough: Compute your workup with fully-loaded CAC first — marketing-only CAC is the most common lie founders tell themselves. Then segment by channel before celebrating.

pitfalls: Marketing-only CAC — salaries and tools are acquisition costs too; excluding them inflates every ratio.
Ignoring payback — a 5:1 ratio with 30-month payback still bankrupts you.
Blended averages — one channel's excellence hiding three channels' waste is the default; segment or stay blind.
lessons.try_it: Build the unit economics workup for your venture with real or estimated numbers. Flag which inputs are guesses — those are your measurement priorities.

lessons.title: Funnels: Mapping the Customer Journey
concepts: A funnel is the staged conversion path from stranger to revenue: visitor → signup → activated → paying → retained. Each stage has a conversion rate, and the product of the rates is your overall efficiency.
Map the funnel from your actual data, not your imagined journey — where users really go, where they stall, where they vanish. Analytics tools show the truth; opinions show the wish.
The biggest absolute drop is not always the priority: a 50%→40% drop on 10,000 people beats a 10%→5% drop on 100 people. Multiply rate gaps by stage volume to find the money.
Funnels leak backward too: poor onboarding (activation) poisons retention months later. Always read the funnel alongside cohort retention before concluding where the problem lives.

example.code:
FUNNEL AUDIT
  Stage        Volume   Conv%   Lost
  Visitors     10,000    —       —
  Signups       1,200   12%    8,800
  Activated       480   40%      720
  Paying          120   25%      360
  Retained(3mo)    84   70%       36
  MONEY LEAK: activation loses 720 of 1,200 — the hunt starts there.
example.walkthrough: Build your funnel audit from real data this week. The stage with the largest absolute loss is your first experiment backlog — everything else waits.

pitfalls: Optimizing the top of the funnel first — more visitors into a leaking funnel is the most expensive mistake in growth.
Trusting the imagined journey — users do not read your onboarding plan; watch what they actually do.
One-time funnel analysis — funnels drift as product and traffic change; audit monthly.
lessons.try_it: Draft your funnel with five stages and fill in real or estimated volumes. Circle the stage you would attack first and write why in one sentence.

lessons.title: Cohort Analysis: Retention Truth
concepts: Cohorts group customers by start period (signup month) so you compare like with like — January's customers at month 3 versus February's at month 3 — instead of mixing new and old users into one misleading average.
The retention curve is the shape of your business: flat curves mean product-market fit compounding; declining curves mean a leaky bucket where growth is rented, not owned.
Compare cohorts across product changes: did the March onboarding revamp actually lift month-2 retention for the April cohort? Cohorts turn opinions about product work into verdicts.
Segment cohorts by acquisition channel and plan tier — enterprise cohorts and self-serve cohorts are different businesses with different curves, and blending them hides both truths.

example.code:
COHORT TABLE (month-N retention %)
           M1   M2   M3   M4
  Jan 24  100%  62%  51%  47%
  Feb 24  100%  58%  44%  —
  Mar 24  100%  71%  —    —   ← onboarding revamp shipped
  READ: Mar cohort retains 13pts better at M2 — the revamp worked.
example.walkthrough: Build one cohort table for your product (or a hypothetical) and read it like the example: which cohort improved, what changed, what is the verdict on that change?

pitfalls: Blended retention averages — mixing January veterans with yesterday's signups produces a number that describes no one.
Celebrating signups while curves decline — acquisition is vanity until a cohort curve flattens.
Too-short windows — B2B retention needs 6-12 month curves; month-1 data proves almost nothing.
lessons.try_it: Sketch a 4×4 cohort table for your venture with plausible numbers. Write the one-sentence verdict a board member would draw from it.

lessons.title: Experimentation: Designing Valid Tests
concepts: Every growth experiment needs four parts: a hypothesis ('changing X will move metric Y because Z'), one variable changed, a defined success metric decided in advance, and enough sample size to trust the result.

Pre-register the success metric and the decision rule before launching — 'we will ship if signup conversion rises 10% relative over two weeks.' Deciding after the data arrives is how teams ship noise.
Run one variable at a time per audience: changing the headline, the price, and the CTA simultaneously teaches you nothing about which one worked.
Kill fast, document always: most experiments fail, and that is the point. A written log of failed tests is an asset — it stops the team from re-running dead ideas every six months.

example.code:
EXPERIMENT CARD
  Hypothesis: [change] → [metric] because [reason]
  Audience: [segment], Sample: [n per variant]
  Metric: [one primary], Guardrail: [metric that must not drop]
  Rule: ship if [threshold] by [date]; kill otherwise
  Result: [data] → Decision: [ship/kill/iterate] → Logged: [date]
example.walkthrough: Write three experiment cards for your biggest funnel leak before running any of them. The discipline of the card — especially the kill rule — is what separates testing from thrashing.

pitfalls: No pre-registered metric — post-hoc metric shopping manufactures false wins.
Testing without enough traffic — a 200-visitor test cannot detect a 10% lift; do the sample math first.
Shipping inconclusive winners — 'trending positive' is not a result; kill or extend, never ship on vibes.
lessons.try_it: Fill out one complete experiment card for your venture's top funnel leak, including the kill rule and the sample size you would need.

lessons.title: Attribution: What Actually Drove Growth
concepts: Attribution answers 'which touchpoint deserves credit for this customer?' — and every model lies differently: last-click over-credits search, first-click over-credits awareness, and multi-touch models argue with each other.
The practical approach: use one consistent model for trend decisions, run holdout experiments for truth. Turn off a channel in one region for a month — the revenue delta is the real attribution.
Beware the correlation trap: customers who read your blog convert better, but blog readers were already more interested. Attribution models routinely credit intent as if it were influence.
For early startups, directional attribution beats precision: know your top two channels by CAC and payback, and do not let perfect measurement delay the obvious reallocation.

example.code:
ATTRIBUTION REALITY CHECK
  Last-click says: search drove 60% of signups
  First-click says: content drove 55% of signups
  Holdout test: pausing search → signups drop 25% (true marginal value)
  DECISION: fund by marginal CAC from holdouts, not by any model's credit split
example.walkthrough: Pick your most expensive channel and design a holdout test for it this quarter. One honest holdout teaches more than a year of model debates.

pitfalls: Model worship — no attribution model is true; they are all lenses, and lenses distort.
Crediting intent as influence — high-intent touchpoints look effective because interested buyers touch them.
Analysis paralysis — early on, directional truth plus fast reallocation beats perfect measurement.
lessons.try_it: List your acquisition channels with last-click credit each. Mark which one you would holdout-test first and what you expect to learn.

lessons.title: The First Ten Hires
concepts: Hires 1-10 define the company's DNA: each one is 10%+ of the culture, so a single mis-hire at this stage does more damage than five mis-hires at employee 200.

Hire for the bottleneck, not the org chart: the next hire should unblock the current constraint — usually either building (engineering) or selling (revenue) — not fill a title you saw at a big company.
Generalists beat specialists early: your fifth employee will do support, QA, docs, and sales calls in one week. Specialists become valuable once the work volume justifies focus.
Sell the mission and the growth, not the salary: you cannot outbid big tech on cash, so recruit on trajectory — candidates who want scope and speed self-select in.

example.code:
FIRST-TEN HIRING FILTER
  1. Bottleneck fit: does this hire unblock our current constraint?
  2. Generalist range: can they do three adjacent jobs this month?
  3. Trajectory hunger: do they want scope more than salary?
  4. Culture add: what do they bring that we lack? (not 'fit in')
  5. Reference check: always call two former managers, always ask 'would you rehire?'
example.walkthrough: Run every candidate through all five filters and write the answers down. The discipline of writing exposes the hires you are rationalizing — and at this stage, one rationalized hire is a company-level risk.

pitfalls: Hiring for titles — 'VP of Sales' at 8 people is theater; hire doers, title later.
Skipping reference checks under time pressure — the 30-minute call that prevents a 6-month mistake is the highest-ROI meeting you will ever hold.
Hiring fast and firing slow — reverse it: hire deliberately, and act quickly when it is not working.
lessons.try_it: Write the job spec for your venture's next most-needed hire using the five-filter format. Identify which filter is hardest to satisfy — that is your sourcing strategy.

lessons.title: Culture as Operating System
concepts: Culture is not perks or posters — it is the set of behaviors that get rewarded when no one is watching. Every promotion, bonus, and tolerated violation writes the real values doc.
Founders install culture through the first ten decisions under pressure: who you promote, who you fire, what you celebrate in all-hands. Teams copy what survives stress, not what is printed.

Write the operating principles early and briefly — five behaviors, each with a concrete example. 'Customer obsession' is a poster; 'we answer support tickets within 2 hours, including weekends' is a culture.
Culture debt compounds like technical debt: the toxic high-performer you tolerate in month 6 becomes the reason your best people leave in month 18.

example.code:
OPERATING PRINCIPLES (example)
  1. Customers before comfort — support SLA 2h, founders take tickets weekly
  2. Write it down — decisions live in docs, not in someone's head
  3. Disagree and commit — debate hard, then execute fully
  4. Default to truth — bad news travels fast here, no surprises
  5. Owners, not renters — if you see it broken, it is yours to fix
example.walkthrough: Draft your five principles with one concrete behavior each. Then audit last month: which principle did your own actions violate? Fix that first — culture starts with the founder's consistency.

pitfalls: Values posters without behaviors — unenforceable values are worse than none; they breed cynicism.
Tolerating brilliant jerks — one toxic high-performer rewrites the culture for everyone watching.
Copying another company's culture — principles must fit your actual constraints, not someone else's blog post.
lessons.try_it: Draft five operating principles for your venture, each with a concrete observable behavior. Test each: could a new hire tell whether they violated it?

lessons.title: Managing When You Are New at It
concepts: First-time founders manage by accident: yesterday you were a peer, today you run 1:1s. The shift is from doing the work to making the work doable for others.
The 1:1 is your core management tool: weekly, 30 minutes, their agenda first. Status updates are the least valuable use — use it for blockers, growth, and early warnings.
Feedback is a system, not an event: specific, timely, and balanced between reinforcement ('keep doing X, it caused Y') and redirection ('when you did X, the effect was Y; try Z').
Delegate outcomes, not tasks: 'own onboarding conversion, target 40% by Q3' beats 'redesign the signup page.' Outcomes create owners; tasks create ticket-takers.

example.code:
1:1 AGENDA (their agenda first)
  1. Wins since last time (2 min — start with energy)
  2. Blockers I can remove (10 min — your main job)
  3. Feedback both ways (10 min — specific, recent, behavioral)
  4. Growth: what are you learning? (8 min — retention lives here)
  NEVER: status readout (that belongs in writing, async)
example.walkthrough: Start weekly 1:1s with this agenda this week, even with one report. The habit matters more than the headcount — by hire ten, you will be fluent.

pitfalls: Canceling 1:1s when busy — the week you most need signal is the week you cancel it.
Managing by task assignment — you become the bottleneck and your team becomes executors.
Saving feedback for reviews — stale feedback is useless feedback; say it within 48 hours.
lessons.try_it: Write the agenda for your next 1:1 (real or hypothetical). Draft one piece of specific behavioral feedback you have been postponing — and deliver it within 48 hours.

lessons.title: Compensation: Cash, Equity, and Fairness
concepts: Startup compensation is a three-legged stool: cash (survival), equity (upside), and growth (career trajectory). You will lose on cash — win decisively on the other two.
Equity grants follow stage norms: first engineers 0.5-2%, later hires 0.05-0.25%, with four-year vesting and a one-year cliff as the universal standard. Deviate deliberately, not accidentally.

Fairness is transparency about philosophy, not equal numbers: publish the compensation philosophy (how levels, cash/equity mix, and refreshers work) so people trust the system even when individual numbers differ.
Refreshers matter more than initial grants for retention: top performers' equity vests out in year 4 — plan refresher grants in year 2-3 or watch them walk at the cliff.

example.code:
OFFER FRAMEWORK
  Cash: market-adjusted for stage (be honest: 'we pay 70th percentile of seed startups')
  Equity: [X]% over 4yr, 1yr cliff — show the dollar value at 3 scenarios
  Growth: the role in 18 months if we hit plan (title, scope, team)
  Philosophy doc: levels, bands, refresher policy — shared with every candidate
  CLOSE: 'You are buying a lottery ticket that we are rigging in our favor together.'
example.walkthrough: Benchmark your equity bands against stage norms before the next offer. Then write the one-page compensation philosophy — it will save you ten painful negotiations.

pitfalls: Equity as an afterthought — vague promises ('we'll take care of you') destroy trust at the first priced round.
Equal grants regardless of role or timing — fairness is principled differentiation, not sameness.
Ignoring refreshers — year-4 vesting cliffs are predictable attrition events; plan for them.
lessons.try_it: Draft the equity component of an offer for a hypothetical first engineer: percentage, vesting, and the three-scenario dollar math you would show them.

lessons.title: The Firing Conversation
concepts: Firing is a leadership obligation, not a cruelty: keeping a mis-hired person harms them (stagnation), the team (morale tax), and the company (missed constraint). Delay is the real cruelty.
The process is humane and fast: clear expectations in writing, a real chance to improve (30-60 day PIP with measurable goals), then a direct, private, same-day conversation if it does not work.

The conversation itself is 10 minutes: the decision is made, state it plainly ('we're letting you go'), explain briefly, cover logistics (severance, references, transition), and do not debate the verdict.
Afterward, tell the team honestly and quickly: acknowledge the departure, reaffirm standards, do not trash the person. How you handle exits teaches everyone what working here means.

example.code:
EXIT SCRIPT
  'I've made the decision to end your employment here, effective today.
  This follows the performance plan we discussed on [date]; the goals weren't met.
  Here's what happens next: [severance], [benefits], [reference policy].
  I want to make the transition respectful — what do you need from me this week?'
  Then: team note within 24h, systems access handled, work redistributed.
example.walkthrough: Rehearse the script out loud once — the words feel foreign until spoken. When the day comes, clarity and kindness are not opposites; the script holds both.

pitfalls: The slow fade — hoping they quit avoids one hard conversation and creates six months of team damage.
Debating the decision in the meeting — the verdict is final; relitigating it is cruel to everyone.
Trash-talking after — the team is watching; your handling of exits is your culture, demonstrated.
lessons.try_it: Write down the performance bar for one role on your team as measurable goals. If someone is below it today, draft their 30-day improvement plan — clarity now prevents crisis later.

lessons.title: When to Sell: Reading the Timing
concepts: Companies are bought, not sold: the best exits come from building something acquirers need, then running a process — not from deciding one day to 'explore strategic alternatives' from weakness.
The three timing windows: when growth is accelerating (maximum valuation), when a strategic shift makes you critical to a buyer (maximum leverage), and before the market turns (maximum prudence).

Selling from strength versus selling from distress is a 3-10x valuation difference. The time to prepare for an exit is 12-18 months before you need one — clean books, documented IP, transferable customer relationships.
Founder readiness is a real variable: burnout, co-founder misalignment, or a life event can make a good offer at the wrong time the right decision. Name your personal walk-away conditions early.

example.code:
EXIT READINESS CHECKLIST (review annually)
  Financials: 3 years clean books, unit economics documented
  Legal: IP assigned, cap table clean, contracts assignable
  Commercial: top-10 customers transferable, no single-customer >25%
  Team: key-person risk documented, retention plan ready
  Personal: founder walk-away number and life-after plan named
example.walkthrough: Run the readiness checklist this quarter even if you never plan to sell. Exit-ready companies are also fundable, acquirable-talent, and simply better-run — the preparation is never wasted.

pitfalls: Planning the exit only when desperate — distress sales transfer all leverage to the buyer.
Ignoring founder readiness — a burned-out founder tanks diligence energy and deal outcomes.
Dirty cap tables and IP — the two diligence killers that crater deals in week three.
lessons.try_it: Score your venture against the five readiness rows. Circle the weakest row and write the 90-day fix.

lessons.title: The Acquirer Landscape
concepts: Strategic acquirers buy what they cannot build fast enough: your customers, your team, your technology, or your market position. They pay strategic premiums — but integrate brutally.
Financial buyers (private equity) buy cash flows and buy them with math: they pay for EBITDA multiples and growth, and they keep the machine running. Lower multiples, cleaner process.
Acqui-hires buy teams, not companies: fast, small, and usually disappointing on price — but sometimes the right outcome for a struggling venture with a great team.

Map your likely buyers before you need them: who has acquired in your space, what did they pay for, and which executive owns M&A? Relationships built over two years beat banker introductions in two weeks.

example.code:
BUYER MAP
  Strategic: [3-5 companies] — motive: [customers/tech/team], buyer: [corp-dev lead]
  Financial: [2-3 PE firms active in space] — motive: [cash flow + growth]
  Acqui-hire: [2-3 talent-hungry players] — fallback, not plan A
  For each: acquisition history, typical multiples, relationship owner, last contact
example.walkthrough: Build your buyer map with five names and one relationship thread each. A quarterly check-in with corp-dev contacts is the cheapest exit preparation that exists.

pitfalls: One-buyer dependency — a single interested acquirer is not a process, it is a hostage situation.
Cold outreach at exit time — buyers pay premiums for companies they have watched, not strangers.
Ignoring financial buyers — PE is often the cleaner, faster close founders overlook.
lessons.try_it: Draft your buyer map: three strategics, two financial buyers, with the motive and relationship owner for each.

lessons.title: Valuation Methods for Startups
concepts: Revenue multiples dominate growth-stage valuation: 5-15x ARR for strong SaaS, adjusted for growth rate, retention, and margins. Growth rate moves the multiple more than anything else.
EBITDA multiples rule profitable companies: 8-20x depending on industry and growth. Unprofitable startups get valued on revenue or not at all — there is no EBITDA math without the E.

Strategic value breaks the comps: a buyer who saves $50M in R&D or captures your $30M revenue stream can justify prices no multiple explains. Your job is to quantify their synergy, not just your financials.

The Berkus-style early methods (scorecard, risk-factor summation) matter pre-revenue: team, product, market, and traction milestones each add defensible value when there are no financials to multiply.

example.code:
VALUATION STACK
  Base: ARR × [5-15x] (growth-adjusted) or EBITDA × [8-20x]
  Adjust: net retention >120% → top of range; churn high → bottom
  Strategic kicker: buyer's quantified synergy (R&D saved, revenue captured)
  Floor: team + IP + customer list value (the acqui-hire math)
  Sanity: last-round valuation × progress multiple — down rounds poison processes
example.walkthrough: Value your company three ways — revenue multiple, strategic synergy, and floor — and note the spread. The spread is your negotiation range; the floor is your walk-away math.

pitfalls: Single-method valuation — one multiple is an opinion; three methods are a negotiating position.
Ignoring the strategic kicker — buyers pay for their synergy, and unquantified synergy goes uncompensated.
Forgetting the last round — pricing below your last valuation starts every conversation with an apology.
lessons.try_it: Run the valuation stack on your venture with estimated numbers. Write the one-paragraph story that justifies the top of your range.

lessons.title: Due Diligence: Surviving the Microscope
concepts: Due diligence is the buyer verifying every claim in your pitch: financials, contracts, IP, cap table, customers, team, tech, and legal. Assume everything will be checked — because it will be.
The data room is the product: organized, complete, and current before the process starts. A messy data room signals a messy company and invites price chips ('we found issues, so...').
Customer diligence is where deals die: buyers call your top customers, and one 'we're evaluating alternatives' can crater valuation. Prep your champions — never surprise them with a buyer's call.

Founder energy is a diligence input: exhausted, defensive founders in week six signal risk. Pace yourself, staff the process, and keep running the business — a dipping quarter mid-diligence is the classic deal-killer.

example.code:
DATA ROOM INDEX
  01 Financials (3yr + projections + unit economics)
  02 Legal (formation, IP assignments, cap table, contracts)
  03 Commercial (customer list, top-10 contracts, pipeline, churn data)
  04 Product/Tech (architecture, security, roadmap, key-person docs)
  05 Team (org chart, comp, retention agreements)
  06 Compliance (licenses, audits, litigation — including none)
example.walkthrough: Start your data room index this month — even a skeleton. Every quarter it stays current is a quarter of future diligence friction removed.

pitfalls: Surprising your customers — buyer calls they did not expect become negative references.
Letting the business dip mid-process — diligence takes 60-90 days; a bad quarter then is catastrophic.
Hiding issues — discovered problems crater trust and price; disclosed problems get solved or discounted once.
lessons.try_it: Draft your data room index with the six sections. Mark which sections are ready today and which would take a month — close the gap on one this quarter.

lessons.title: Negotiation: Terms Beyond Price
concepts: Headline price is one term among many: cash vs stock, escrow holdbacks, earnouts, founder vesting, retention packages, and reps-and-warranties liability shape what you actually take home.

Earnouts — 'we'll pay $X more if you hit targets' — are where acquirers move risk to you: most earnouts underpay because post-acquisition you control neither the resources nor the accounting. Discount promised earnouts steeply.
Founder vesting and retention: expect 2-4 year vesting on your equity and employment agreements. Negotiate the role, the reporting line, and the walk-away — golden handcuffs chafe.
Process creates leverage: two credible bidders beat one brilliant negotiator. Never negotiate exclusively until the price and key terms are set — exclusivity is given, not assumed.

example.code:
TERM SHEET BEYOND PRICE (checklist)
  Consideration: cash % vs stock % (stock = buyer risk)
  Escrow: 10-15% holdback, 12-24 months (negotiate the cap)
  Earnout: targets YOU control, measured YOUR way, or refuse it
  Founder deal: vesting years, role, reporting line, severance
  Reps & warranties: cap liability, survival period, disclosure schedules
  Exclusivity: only after price + key terms agreed, max 30-45 days
example.walkthrough: Memorize the beyond-price checklist. In your next hypothetical acquisition, write which three terms you would fight hardest for — price is rarely all three.

pitfalls: Price-only focus — a $50M headline with a 50% earnout and 4-year vesting can be worth less than $35M cash.
Granting exclusivity early — exclusivity without agreed terms is unilateral disarmament.
Accepting uncontrollable earnouts — targets measured by the buyer's accounting are lottery tickets, not compensation.
lessons.try_it: Take a hypothetical $40M acquisition offer and restructure it three ways: all-cash, cash+stock, cash+earnout. Compute your real take-home under each in a downside case.

lessons.title: Life After the Exit
concepts: The wire transfer is the beginning of a new problem set: identity ('who am I without the company?'), structure (the 60-hour weeks are gone), and relationships (the team scatters, some friendships do not survive).
Plan the first 90 days post-close before the close: rest deliberately, then structured exploration — advising, angel investing, or the next idea — on a timeline, not a drift.

Wealth management is unglamorous and urgent: tax planning before the close (not after), diversification out of the acquirer's stock, and a fiduciary advisor — not your college roommate with stock tips.

The best second acts compound the first: founders who stay in their domain as angels, advisors, or operators outperform those who chase novelty. Your network and pattern recognition are the assets — deploy them.

example.code:
POST-EXIT 90-DAY PLAN
  Days 1-30: REST — no big decisions, health reset, family time (scheduled, not vague)
  Days 31-60: EXPLORE — 20 conversations: founders, investors, operators in your domain
  Days 61-90: COMMIT — pick one vehicle: advise (portfolio), invest (angel), build (nextco)
  Parallel: tax plan executed, stock diversified, advisor retained, estate docs updated
example.walkthrough: Write your post-exit plan now — hypothetically. Founders who plan the after before the deal make better deal decisions, because they are not negotiating from existential need.

pitfalls: No plan for the after — the drift after a big exit destroys more founders than failure does.
Post-close tax surprises — structure and timing decisions made before close save seven figures; after close they are history.
Identity collapse — 'former founder of X' is a chapter, not an epitaph; plan the next one deliberately.
lessons.try_it: Draft your 90-day post-exit plan in the template format. Name the one vehicle (advise, invest, build) you would most likely choose and why.

labs.title: Unit economics verdict engine
labs.objective: Extend the lesson's unit-economics function into a script that evaluates three pricing scenarios for a hypothetical startup and prints which (if any) is fundable on unit economics alone.

At least one improved scenario should reach HEALTHY.

labs.title: Problem-discovery interview plan

steps: Create discovery.md: 8 interview questions that uncover problem frequency, cost, current workarounds, and budget ownership — no questions about your solution allowed.

Print both files to the terminal to review them as a founder would before a build decision.

Name the riskiest assumption explicitly in mvp.md.

sections.title: Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track — Core path

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you identified a real customer problem — not one you assumed.
points: Describe the discovery method: who you talked to, what you asked, what surprised you
Show the evidence that the problem was real: frequency, cost, workarounds, budget
Explain what you built or changed because of what you learned
pitfalls: A problem you never validated with actual customers
Skipping the surprise — discovery without surprise is confirmation bias
No link between the learning and the action

behavioral.prompt: Describe your biggest failure as a builder or founder and what it taught you.
points: Own the failure plainly: what you did, what it cost in time or money
Name the specific mistake in method (skipped discovery, ignored unit economics, scaled too early)
Show the changed behavior: what you do differently now, with an example
pitfalls: A humblebrag failure with no real cost
Blaming the market, the team, or timing
No demonstrated change in method

behavioral.prompt: Walk me through how you'd validate a startup idea in two weeks with $500.
points: Start with the riskiest assumption and the cheapest test for it
Show the weekly cadence: interviews, landing page, concierge MVP, metrics
Name the kill criteria: what evidence would make you stop
pitfalls: Spending the $500 on logo and incorporation
No falsifiable criteria
Two weeks of building with no customer contact

behavioral.prompt: Explain unit economics to a non-technical co-founder in two minutes.
points: Use a single concrete customer: what they cost to acquire, what they pay over their lifetime
State the verdict rule plainly: LTV must beat CAC, 3-to-1 is healthy
Connect it to their decisions: why this governs how fast you can grow
pitfalls: Jargon without the example
No verdict rule given
Longer than two minutes

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a disagreement with a co-founder or partner and how you resolved it.
points: Describe the disagreement on its merits, fairly representing their side
Show the resolution mechanism: data, customer evidence, or a reversible experiment — not authority
Name what the partnership learned about deciding together
pitfalls: Painting the other person as irrational
Resolving by fiat or by who cared more
No mechanism for the next disagreement

behavioral.prompt: Why do you want to be a founder instead of joining a great team?
points: Give the real reason: the specific problem you can't not work on, or the craft you want to own end-to-end
Show you understand the trade: lower pay, higher variance, total accountability
Demonstrate founder traits with evidence: shipped things, recruited people, survived uncertainty
pitfalls: 'Be my own boss' as the whole answer
No evidence of building anything
Ignoring the downside of the trade

behavioral.prompt: Pitch your startup idea in 60 seconds.
points: Problem: who hurts, how often, what it costs them — in one sentence
Solution: what you do differently, in one sentence
Proof: the strongest evidence you have (users, revenue, LOIs)
Ask: what you want from this listener, specifically
pitfalls: Leading with features instead of the problem
No proof offered
No ask at the end

behavioral.prompt: What would you do if your startup's unit economics turned out to be broken after launch?
points: Show the diagnostic: which lever — CAC, churn, pricing, margin — is actually broken, with numbers
Sequence the fixes by cost and reversibility: pricing tests before rebuilds
Name the shutdown criterion: when you'd stop rather than burn more capital
pitfalls: 'Raise more money to grow through it'
No diagnostic — jumping to a fix
No willingness to consider shutting down

cheatsheet.title: Entrepreneurship: The Babson-Informed Track — field reference

sections.heading: The discipline
items: Entrepreneurship = method for discovering problems and testing solutions under uncertainty
Method improves cost-per-experiment and odds; it does not remove risk
Foundations audit: finance, marketing, operations — before scale

sections.heading: Venture building
items: Problem discovery: real, frequent, expensive, budgeted — interviews before code
MVP: smallest test of the riskiest assumption; concierge / Wizard-of-Oz / landing page
Kill criteria decided in advance; pivots are data-driven, not emotional

sections.heading: Unit economics
items: LTV = ARPU x gross margin / churn; healthy LTV/CAC >= 3
Growth on broken unit economics scales losses

sections.heading: Fundraising literacy
items: Dilution = raise / post-money; option pool usually comes from founders
1x liquidation preference: investors paid first in a modest exit
Negotiate the package (dilution, control, downside), not just valuation

glossary.def: Structured customer research establishing that a pain is real, frequent, expensive, and budgeted — done before building.
Minimum viable product: the smallest thing that tests the riskiest assumption, not a stripped-down version of the vision.
The per-customer profit math: lifetime value versus acquisition cost, payback period, and contribution margin.
Lifetime value divided by customer acquisition cost; below 1.0 the business loses money per customer, 3.0+ is healthy.
A term-sheet provision paying investors back (typically 1x their investment) before common shareholders in an exit.
The practice of topping up the employee option pool pre-money, so the dilution comes from founders' shares rather than investors'.
Programs taught by working operators rather than academics, trading theory for current field practice.
Pre-committed evidence thresholds that trigger abandoning or pivoting an idea — decided before emotional attachment sets in.
